THE CHINA PRESS, FRIDAY, JUNE 5, 1936

COMMENT ON JUDD
LETTER

Editor, THE CHINA PRESS
Sir: The following passages appeared in the letter of Mr. W.A. Judd recently published in some of the local papers:
“Peters and I were shown every consideration while being detained pending our trial in the Civil Wing of Ward Road Gaol away from the prison proper.”
“Our legal practitioners called whilst we were being detained often after 5 p.m., and regardless of regulation, they were allowed to see us.”
If Mr. Judd’s above statement is to be taken as truth then it would appear that not even foreign prisoners are treated alike in the Ward Road Gaol. Prisoners under criminal charges may be lodged in the Civil Wing and prison regulations may be disregarded at will by those in charge.
Mr. Judd’s statement must be true for it was based partly on his own testimony that he and his associate were acquitted.
It was pointed out to me by a doubting Thomas friend that the statements of Mr. Judd and Mr. Peters do not seem to agree and it was held that one of them may have even fibbed. It was further argued that if inaccuracies or untruths could have crept in on such a simple matter as prison treatment, etc., how could they be depended upon to give a truthful and accurate account of what actually did happen that wintry night when a poor Chinese beggar received his fatal immersion in the Soochow Creek?
I would attribute the discrepancies to the inaccuracies of the reporters or to cable mutilation and would abide without the slightest doubt by the decision which was so favorably received by some of the British Community where the decision was loudly applauded, creating thereby a precedent in the annals of British jurisprudence.
Moreover, even if our ex-police officers were guilty of the crime they were charged with they did very little harm except to their own conscience and to the prestige of the nation from whence they came. The victim, the poor beggar, was beyond harming. His lot was miserable and his death was his release.
KAO KWOK.
Shanghai, June 3, 1936.
page_data.zh:
《字林西报》，1936年6月5日，星期五

评贾德来信

致《字林西报》编辑：
先生：W.A. 贾德（W.A. Judd）先生最近在当地一些报纸上发表的信件中出现了以下段落：
“彼得斯（Peters）和我在提篮桥监狱民事监区（Civil Wing of Ward Road Gaol）候审期间，远离普通囚犯监区，受到了各种优待。”
“在我们被拘留期间，我们的律师经常在下午5点以后来访，尽管违反规定，他们仍被允许会见我们。”
如果贾德先生的上述陈述被视为事实，那么似乎连外国囚犯在提篮桥监狱也没有受到同等对待。刑事指控的囚犯可能被关押在民事监区，而主管人员可以随意无视监狱规章。
贾德先生的陈述必须是真实的，因为这部分基于他自己的证词，即他和他的同伴被判无罪。
一位多疑的朋友向我指出，贾德先生和彼得斯先生的陈述似乎并不一致，有人认为其中一人甚至可能撒了谎。进一步的观点是，如果在监狱待遇等如此简单的事情上都可能出现不准确或不实之词，那么怎能指望他们就那个寒冷的夜晚一名可怜的中国乞丐在苏州河遭受致命溺水这一实际发生的事件提供真实准确的描述呢？
我将这些差异归因于记者的不准确报道或电报传输错误，并毫无疑问地接受那项在英国侨民社区中广受好评、赢得热烈掌声的判决，从而在英国司法史上开创了一个先例。
此外，即使我们的前警官犯下了被指控的罪行，除了对他们自己的良心以及他们所属国家的声誉造成损害外，并没有造成多大危害。受害者，那位可怜的乞丐，已无法再受伤害。他的命运悲惨，死亡对他而言是一种解脱。
高国（KAO KWOK，音译）。
上海，1936年6月3日。

THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, TUESDAY, JUNE 2. 1936

ECHO OF THE PETERS-
JUDD CASE

Mr. Judd Corrects Statements
Made in England

Mr. W. A. Judd wishes to correct
certain statements alleged to have
been made in England by Mr. E.
W. Peters in regard to the treatment
received by Mr. Peters and Mr. Judd
during their detention for trial in the
recent case in the Supreme Court.
The statement in question was not
published in the "North-China Daily
News" but references to it have been
made in other papers and Mr. Judd
wishes it to be known that he and Mr.
Peters were shown every considera-
tion whilst being detained in the Ward
Road Gaol, and Mr. Judd wishes again
to thank the Gaol staff for their con-
sideration. He goes on to say:
Regarding lawyer's fees, Peters paid
exactly the same as I, as Peters' fees
were paid the same time as mine, which
was $250.00 for six days in the Police
Court and $300.00 for eight days in
the Supreme Court, and included out-
side-of-Court work.
These fees, I think, were exceptional-
ly low, and I believe would not even
pay overhead expenses for any lawyer.
My father, thinking I would not have
enough money for lawyer's fees, cabled
£20 to my lawyer, who handed same
to me intact. Our legal practitioners
called whilst we were being detained,
bringing books, newspapers and perio-
dicals for us to read, often after 8
p.m. and they were allowed to see us.
After our resignations had been accept-
ed we were paid all moneys due to
us and we were both granted second-
class passages back to England via any
route. Peters took the Siberian route
and I, not wishing to return to England,
stayed here and am now working in a
clerical capacity for Clarke's Inquiry
and Protection Agency, and not "far
away up country."

（批：file / YR）
（批：Ghs）

《字林西报》，1936年6月2日，星期二

彼得斯-贾德案余波

贾德先生更正
在英国的言论

W. A. 贾德先生希望更正据称由 E. W. 彼得斯（E. W. Peters）先生在英国就彼得斯先生和贾德先生在近期最高法院案件候审期间所受待遇问题所作的某些陈述。
该争议陈述并未刊登在《字林西报》上，但其他报纸曾提及此事，贾德先生希望公众知悉，他和彼得斯先生在提篮桥监狱被拘留期间受到了各种优待，贾德先生再次感谢监狱工作人员的关照。他接着说：
关于律师费，彼得斯支付的费用与我完全相同，因为彼得斯的费用是与我的费用同时支付的，即在警察法庭六天的费用为250.00美元，在最高法院八天的费用为300.00美元，其中包括庭外工作费用。
我认为这些费用异常低廉，相信甚至不足以支付任何律师的管理开支。我父亲认为我没有足够的钱支付律师费，便给我的律师汇去了20英镑，律师将这笔钱原封不动地交给了我。我们的法律从业者在我们就押期间前来探访，为我们带来书籍、报纸和期刊供阅读，经常在晚上8点以后，并且他们被允许会见我们。
在我们的辞呈被接受后，我们获得了所有应付款项，并且我们都获准经由任何路线乘坐二等舱返回英国。彼得斯选择了西伯利亚路线，而我不愿返回英国，留在这里，目前在克拉克调查与保护社（Clarke's Inquiry and Protection Agency）担任文员工作，并非“远在内地”。

（批：归档 / YR）
（批：Ghs）

THE SHANGHAI TIMES, TUESDAY, JUNE 2, 1936.
CORRECTING STATEMENT
Editor,
THE SHANGHAI TIMES
Sir,—With reference to a state-
ment made by Ernest William
Peters at Dover, England, on April
15 and re-published by some
papers locally, I would like to
bring to your notice one or two
errors made by him in that state-
ment.
Firstly, I will quote parts of
his statement:—"I spent five weeks
in a Shanghai prison. The cell
was tiny and cold, the bed was
hard and the food was scanty.
Everywhere in the prison it was
known that we were Police and
the warders treated us more
strictly than other prisoners lest
it be thought we were receiving
favours.
"I saw the £200 I had paid into
the superannuation fund disappear
in paying for my defence. The
£200 which would have been added
by the authorities was withheld.
"I obtained a third class passage
back across Siberia."
"The other officer who was with
me met with the same treatment;
he, however, had a good friend
who got him a post up country
far away from the scene of our
trial."
The following are a few authen-
tic facts from the officer who was
with him: Peters and I were
shown every consideration whilst
being detained pending our trial
in the Civil Wing of Ward Road
Gaol away from the prison proper.
On the third day of our detention
the senior Warder came and told
us that a number of the foreign
members of the Gaol Staff had
asked for and received permission
to send us three meals a day, from
their own mess, for which they
themselves would pay. I take this
opportunity to thank them again.
Regarding lawyer's fees, Peters
paid exactly the same as I, as
Peters' fees were paid the same
time as mine, which was $250 for
six days in the Police Court and
$300 for eight days in the Supreme
Court, and included outside-of-
Court work.
These fees, I think, were excep-
tionally low, and I believe would
not even pay overhead expenses
for any lawyer. My Father, think-
ing I would not have enough money
for lawyer's fees, cabled £20 to
my lawyer, who handed same to
me intact. Our legal practitioners
called whilst we were being de-
tained, bringing books, news-
papers and periodicals for us to
read; often after 5 p.m. and,
regardless of regulations, they
were allowed to see us.
After our resignations had been
accepted we were paid all moneys
due to us and we were both grant-
ed second-class passages back to
England via any route. Peters
took the Siberian route and I, not
wishing to return to England,
stayed here and am now working
in a clerical capacity for Clarke's
Inquiry and Protection Agency,
and not "far away up country."
W. A. JUDD.
Shanghai, May 30, 1936.

更正声明

致
《上海泰晤士报》编辑
先生，——鉴于欧内斯特·威廉·彼得斯（Ernest William Peters）于4月15日在英国多佛发表并由当地一些报纸转载的声明，我想提请贵报注意他在该声明中犯下的一两个错误。
首先，我引用他声明的部分内容：“我在上海监狱度过了五周。牢房狭小寒冷，床铺坚硬，食物匮乏。监狱里人人都知道我们是警察，狱警对我们比其他囚犯更严厉，以免被人认为我们受到了优待。
“我看到我存入养老基金的200英镑在支付辩护费用时化为乌有。当局本应追加的200英镑也被扣留。
“我获得了一张经西伯利亚返回的三等舱船票。”
“与我在一起的另一名警官受到了同样的待遇；然而，他有一位好朋友，为他谋得了一份远离我们审判现场的内地职位。”
以下是与他在一起的那位警官提供的一些确凿事实：彼得斯和我在提篮桥监狱民事监区候审期间，远离普通囚犯监区，受到了各种优待。在我们被拘留的第三天，高级狱警前来告诉我们，多名外籍监狱工作人员已申请并获准从他们自己的食堂每天为我们提供三餐，费用由他们自己承担。我借此机会再次向他们表示感谢。
关于律师费，彼得斯支付的费用与我完全相同，因为彼得斯的费用是与我的费用同时支付的，即在警察法庭六天的费用为250美元，在最高法院八天的费用为300美元，其中包括庭外工作费用。
我认为这些费用异常低廉，相信甚至不足以支付任何律师的管理开支。我父亲认为我没有足够的钱支付律师费，便给我的律师汇去了20英镑，律师将这笔钱原封不动地交给了我。我们的法律从业者在我们就押期间前来探访，为我们带来书籍、报纸和期刊供阅读；经常在下午5点以后，并且尽管违反规定，他们仍被允许会见我们。
在我们的辞呈被接受后，我们获得了所有应付款项，并且我们都获准经由任何路线乘坐二等舱返回英国。彼得斯选择了西伯利亚路线，而我不愿返回英国，留在这里，目前在克拉克调查与保护社担任文员工作，并非“远在内地”。
W. A. 贾德。
上海，1936年5月30日。

THE CHINA PRESS, SATURDAY, MAY 16, 1936

Former S.M.P. Sergeant In
Dover Talks Of Trial Here

E. W. Peters Says Jail Cell Tiny, Cold And
Food Scanty; Man Freed On Murder Count
Declares “I Will Not Whine”

While William Alfred Judd, former probationary sergeant of the Shanghai Municipal Police, is now working in Shanghai as a private detective, Ernest William Peters, former S.M.P. sergeant, who was faced with Judd last February of charges of having murdered a beggar, is now back home in England, ready to start life over again and with very little in the way of capital to help him along.

According to a Dover newspaper, Peters reached that city on April 15 with only 11 pence and a half-penny in his pocket. He had returned to England by way of the Trans-Siberian Railway.

Peters and Judd figured prominently in the headlines of local newspapers early this year, when they were tried before Judge A. G. Mossop and a jury of 12 men, on a charge of having murdered Mau Teh-piau, a beggar, by throwing him into Hongkew Creek early one morning in December. After a trial lasting more than a week, the jury turned in a verdict of “not guilty.”

Held In Detention Cells

Both men were given their freedom on bail during the preliminary investigation held before Registrar C. H. Haines in H. M. Police Court, but were sent back to a detention cell when charges of murder were preferred against them.

On his arrival in Dover, Peters granted a press interview, the first he gave since his arrest. The interview follows:

“I will not whine,” he said, “although I have lost everything. My job has gone. I have forfeited the pension I was looking forward to at the conclusion of my police service.

“I had been promoted sergeant after only six years’ service, and I was expecting further promotion. I left the Tank Corps with an exemplary character, and joined the Shanghai police. For a time I was with the riot squad, and took part in many fierce fights.”

Referring to the hardships of his journey across Russia and Siberia, he related: “Many days I was hungry, and the hard boards were none too comfortable. And all this was on top of the five weeks I spent in a Shanghai prison. The story really starts in the early hours of the first day of last December. I was on duty in the station to which I was attached. Another officer new to the district was with me. News reached us that a Chinese was lying sick near a creek. Night after night we had received similar messages from Chinese anxious to receive attention.

Off we went to see to this latest report. Ordinarily the other officer would have gone alone, but as he was new to the district I accompanied him. We found a Chinese named Mau Teh-piau. There seemed to be something wrong with him, so we carried him to the side of the Hongkew creek and put him into one of the scores of ‘beggar boats’ that lie close to the bank.

“Bed Hard . . . Food Scanty”

“We had to lean over a railing and drop him about two feet. We had been taken to the spot in a police car driven by a Chinese police driver, who later made a statement that the other officer and I deliberately threw Plau (Mau) into the creek. Plau (Mau) was fished out of the creek, but evidence was produced at the trial proving that Plau (Mau) was seen after we had left the spot, and that he threw himself into the creek because he was starving and destitute. But Plau (Mau) died in hospital, and I was arrested and put on my trial accused of murder.

“At first I was granted bail, but subsequently, and until I came before the Supreme Court, I spent five weeks in a Shanghai prison. The cell was tiny and cold. The bed was hard and the food was scanty. Everywhere in the prison it was known that we were police, and the warders treated us more strictly than other prisoners, lest it be thought we were receiving favors.

Free—But Ruined

“It was a weary five weeks. I saw that whatever the outcome of the case I could never hope to be reinstated in the police service. I saw the £200 I had paid into the superannuation fund disappear in paying for my defense. The £200 which would have been added to my £200 by the authorities was withheld. I thanked God I was a single man. The case dragged on. Very contradictory evidence was given. Then I was found not guilty. I was free—but ruined. I obtained a third class passage back across Siberia. The little money I had for food was not nearly enough. I missed more meals than I had. I asked the authorities to appeal to the Foreign Office to see what could be done but this request was refused. The other officer who was with me met with the same treatment. He, however, had a good friend out there, who got him a post up country far away from the scene of our trial. Friends have advised me to get the matter brought up in Parliament. Anyhow, at 32, I am facing the world again with a first-class Army character, with an excellent and unblemished record of service in the police—and 11 pence half-penny.”

《字林西报》，1936年5月16日，星期六

前上海公共租界工部局警务处巡长在
多佛谈论在此地的审判

E. W. 彼得斯称牢房狭小、寒冷且
食物匮乏；谋杀指控获释者
宣称“我不会抱怨”

当上海公共租界工部局警务处（S.M.P.）前见习巡长威廉·阿尔弗雷德·贾德（William Alfred Judd）现在上海作为一名私家侦探工作时，前上海公共租界工部局警务处巡长欧内斯特·威廉·彼得斯（Ernest William Peters）——今年二月曾与贾德一同面临谋杀一名乞丐的指控——现已回到英国老家，准备重新开始生活，但几乎没有资本帮助他起步。

据多佛的一家报纸报道，彼得斯于4月15日抵达该市，口袋里只有11.5便士。他是经西伯利亚铁路返回英国的。

今年年初，彼得斯和贾德在当地报纸的头版新闻中占据显著位置，当时他们在法官A. G. 莫索普（A. G. Mossop）和由12人组成的陪审团面前受审，被指控于12月的一个清晨将乞丐毛德彪（Mau Teh-piau，音译）扔进虹口港（Hongkew Creek）。经过为期一周多的审判，陪审团作出了“无罪”裁决。

被关押在拘留所

在 registrar C. H. 海恩斯（C. H. Haines）主持的皇家警察法庭初步调查期间，两人均获保释自由，但当谋杀指控正式提出后，他们又被送回拘留所。

抵达多佛后，彼得斯接受了媒体采访，这是自他被捕以来首次接受采访。采访内容如下：

“我不会抱怨，”他说，“虽然我失去了一切。我的工作没了。我失去了原本期待在警察生涯结束时获得的养老金。

“我在仅服役六年后就被提升为巡长，并期待着进一步的晋升。我离开坦克兵团时品行模范，随后加入了上海警察队伍。有一段时间我在防暴队服役，参与了许多激烈的战斗。”

谈到穿越俄罗斯和西伯利亚旅途的艰辛，他叙述道：“许多天我都饿着肚子，坚硬的木板床一点也不舒服。而这一切还是在我上海监狱度过的五周之后发生的。故事实际上始于去年12月第一天的凌晨。我在所属的警局值班。另一名对该地区不熟悉的新警官与我在一起。我们收到消息，有一名中国人病倒在一条小河附近。接连几个晚上，我们都收到渴望得到关注的中国人发来的类似消息。

我们出发去处理这最新的报告。通常另一名警官会独自前往，但由于他对该地区不熟悉，我陪同他一起去了。我们发现了一名名叫毛德彪的中国人。他看起来有些不对劲，于是我们将他抬到虹口港边，把他放进停靠在岸边的众多‘乞丐船’中的一艘里。

“床铺坚硬……食物匮乏”

“我们必须探身越过栏杆，将他放下约两英尺深。我们是由一名中国警察司机驾驶的警车带到现场的，该司机后来作证称，另一名警官和我故意将毛（Plau/Mau）扔进河里。毛（Plau/Mau）从河里被捞起，但在审判中提出的证据证明，在我们离开现场后有人看到过毛（Plau/Mau），并且他是因饥饿和贫困而跳河自尽的。但毛（Plau/Mau）在医院去世，我被捕并以谋杀罪受审。

“起初我获准保释，但随后，直到我出庭最高法院之前，我在上海监狱度过了五周。牢房狭小寒冷。床铺坚硬，食物匮乏。监狱里人人都知道我们是警察，狱警对我们比其他囚犯更严厉，以免被人认为我们受到了优待。

自由——但已毁灭

“那是疲惫不堪的五周。我意识到，无论案件结果如何，我都绝无希望复职警察队伍。我看到我存入养老基金的200英镑在支付辩护费用时化为乌有。当局本应在我缴纳的200英镑基础上追加的200英镑也被扣留。我感谢上帝我还是个单身汉。案件拖延了很久。证词非常矛盾。然后我被判无罪。我自由了——但也毁了。我获得了一张经西伯利亚返回的三等舱船票。我仅有的一点买食物的钱远远不够。我错过的饭比我吃到的还多。我请求当局向外交部呼吁，看看能做些什么，但这一请求被拒绝了。与我在一起的另一名警官受到了同样的待遇。然而，他在那里有一位好朋友，为他谋得了一份远离我们审判现场的内地职位。朋友们建议我将此事提交议会讨论。无论如何，32岁的我正以一流的军队品行证明、在警察队伍中优秀且无瑕疵的服务记录——以及11.5便士，再次面对这个世界。”

China Times and other local newspapers.

COLLECTION OF AVIATION CONTRIBUTIONS FROM LOCAL BOATS

In Shanghai there are about 20,000 boats
operating on the Huangpoo River and the Soochow Creek.
The China National Aviation Corporation has now established
a "Collection Office of Aviation Contributions from
Local Boats" on the 5th floor of the Flour Exchange
Building on Min Kuo Road. Officials will be detailed

两名警察案

很遗憾，我未能有机会细读本案判决书全文，但我认为判决中可能包含这样的表述：“死者因不会游泳而丧命”，因为这两名外籍警察被指控将其扔入一条小河中。

Star Evening News (星夜報) published the following comment
on February 23:-

THE SUFFERINGS OF A SEMI-COLONIAL COUNTRY

Early on the morning of December 1, 1935,
Peters and Judd, two British policemen of the Shanghai
Municipal Police, threw a sick beggar named Ma Tuh Piao
(馬德標) into the Hongkew Creek, thereby causing his
death. The two policemen were charged and the British
Court found them "Not Guilty" on February 11. The two
accused have since been permitted to resign and it is
reported that they will return to their country in a
few days.
How shall we express our feelings upon learning
of this news?
The citizens of a semi-colonial country have
lost the protection to which they are entitled and their
lives are not worth a cent. Who will ever come forward
for justice and give an impartial decision when a Chinese
has been killed or has suffered some grievance? Who is
there to protect us or to help us? When a Chinese is
killed, there the matter usually ends for nothing is
ever done.
Such are our sufferings when our country is
yet a semi-colony; what will they be after our country
has been annihilated?
Rise! We cannot tolerate any further insult
and oppression at the hands of any foreign Power.
Let us make preparations and struggle for our emancipation!
Let us bear in mind one thing: if we desire
life, we must suffer. Let us then prepare to fight
for our existence!

Star Evening News and other local newspapers:

THE REPORTED KIDNAPPING OF THE SON OF A CERTAIN PROMINENT
LOCAL PERSON

The "Mainichi", a local Japanese newspaper,
has published a report to the effect that the son of a
certain prominent local person has been kidnapped and
that the kidnappers have demanded a sum of $2,000,000
for the return of his son.
The Editor's Remarks: Is this report true
or not? It frightens us. According to the Japanese
paper, the kidnapping took place many days ago. As
no such report has been published by Chinese newspapers,
the Japanese report is probably baseless. If it is true,
then it is indeed the biggest kidnapping case that has
occurred in recent years.

《星夜报》于2月23日发表了以下评论：-

半殖民地国家的苦难

1935年12月1日凌晨，上海公共租界工部局警务处的两名英国警察彼得斯和贾德，将一名名叫马德标（音译）的患病乞丐扔进虹口港，导致其死亡。这两名警察被起诉，英国法院于2月11日裁定他们“无罪”。此后，两名被告获准辞职，据悉他们将在几天后回国。
得知此消息，我们该如何表达我们的感受？
半殖民地国家的公民失去了他们应得的保护，他们的生命一文不值。当中国人被杀或遭受冤屈时，谁会站出来主持公道并做出公正的裁决？谁来保护我们或帮助我们？当中国人被杀时，事情通常就此结束，没有任何后续行动。
这就是我们的国家仍是半殖民地时的苦难；如果我们的国家被灭亡了，苦难又会是怎样？
起来！我们再也不能容忍任何外国列强对我们的侮辱和压迫。
让我们做好准备，为争取我们的解放而斗争！
让我们牢记一点：如果我们想要生存，就必须忍受苦难。那么，让我们为生存而战做好准备吧！

Modern Daily News ( 时代日报 ), a mosquito paper, published
the following comment on February 15:-

A POOR MAN'S LIFE

A Chinese proverb says, "To the poor life is
precious; to the rich, money is precious". But this
proverb is untrue because a poor man's life is not worth
a cent.

The duty of a policeman is to protect the
people, but this is not always so, as, for example, in
the case of the two foreign policemen who threw a sick
beggar into a creek. These policemen not only had
failed to protect the people, but they took a poor man's
life.

We do not know whether the policemen actually
threw the beggar into a creek, but as the Settlement
police had charged them, it would seem that it was not
exactly without foundation. We are ignorant of the
records on which the British Court found the policemen not
guilty, for nothing had been published by the newspapers.
What we can say is that certain people will regard England
as a country of savages. At law, the rich and the poor
are equal, but in reality wealth makes a great difference.
In the present case, the victim is a beggar of a semi-
colony, while the culprits are policemen of a great Power.
Life is thus only precious to the poor them-
selves.

小报《时代日报》于2月15日发表了以下评论：-

穷人的性命

中国有句谚语说，“穷人惜命，富人惜财”。但这句谚语并不正确，因为穷人的性命一文不值。

警察的职责是保护人民，但情况并非总是如此，例如那两名将患病乞丐扔进河里的外籍警察案。这些警察不仅未能保护人民，反而夺走了一条穷人的性命。

我们不知道警察是否真的将乞丐扔进了河里，但由于租界警察对他们提出了指控，看来此事并非毫无根据。我们不了解英国法院裁定警察无罪所依据的记录，因为报纸上没有公布任何相关内容。我们可以说的是，某些人会将英国视为野蛮人之国。在法律上，富人和穷人是平等的，但在现实中，财富造成了巨大的差异。在本案中，受害者是半殖民地的一个乞丐，而罪犯是大国的警察。因此，生命只对穷人自己来说是宝贵的。

page_data.en:
The Shanghai Evening Post & Mercury, Friday, February 14, 1936 2 36

Juries And Justice
To the Editor:
The question of a jury trial has been raised in connection with the recent case here, and this raises the vital difference between the British and American courts here. Both courts follow, in large part, the same English law. But whereas in the one court a defendant can demand trial by jury as in the homeland, in the other court trial by jury has so far been customarily and consistently denied.
Raven and Brown have been convicted for offenses against other Americans. But there are cases which involve other nationals, our Chinese hosts for instance.
What is really in the mind of a juror when he sits in a case in which a fellow-national is charged with an offense against a man of some nation or group which the juror considers inferior to his own? How many jurors in China go into the box with the solemn and high resolve to see justice done, whoever is hurt? How many have any real respect for the law, any real respect for the good name of the court in which they serve? How many have any idea of giving, in a foreign land, an example of free and equal justice which will serve as a light and a model for other peoples, and in which they can themselves take pride?
Trial by jury is one of the inestimable achievements of democracy. The right of a man to demand the judgment of his peers is an invaluable bulwark against the arrogance or oppression of officialdom. But when, as in China, special conditions give some national group the position of a privileged class, above the law of the land and subject only to our own laws, special responsibilities are involved. Above all is the responsibility of maintaining even-handed justice, of equality before the law, of courts and jurors showing themselves above personal favor and personal prejudice. Only by so doing, only by showing their possession of a strict sense of justice and equity superior to that of native courts, can extraterritorial courts in any way justify their existence.
I wonder how many jurors, in cases were their own nationals are charged with serious offenses against natives, ever consider such things. How many have any pride in our free institutions, any instinct of loyalty to these institutions? How many go into the jury box with a sense of the stern responsibility that is upon them,—the responsibility of showing, in an alien land and with the eyes of millions upon them, that their own courts are courts of justice, courts of law, the honor and good name of which must be upheld by the jurymen in whose hands lie the decision of cases? How many jurymen out here are guided by such understanding and such principles?
The history of extraterritoriality in China reveals some of the most terrible travesties on justice ever perpetrated. Extraterritorial nationals have been charged—charges often supported by the most complete and damning evidence—with most serious crimes, including murder, rape, armed robbery, counterfeiting. But never has any White man, in our extraterritorial courts, been sentenced to any heavy penalty in consequence. There is a widespread idea among foreigners here that White men would lose prestige by punishing their nationals for grave offenses against China. But a juror believing that, on that account, offenders should escape justice, has no right in the jury box. He perjures himself and besmirches the court by his very acceptance of jury duty. He has no intention of applying even-handed justice; he is in fact incapable of it. He is as rotten, as corrupt, as dishonest as a judge who permits money to determine his decision.
Millions of Chinese follow every case, in extraterritorial courts, concerning grave offenses of foreigners against Chinese. They are curious and anxious to see just how these courts, with their avowed superiority and high standards of equity, really dispense the "even-handed justice" in which we take pride. And the net outcome, in almost all cases, is bitter Chinese hatred for the foreign courts which burlesque justice and protect criminals, and utter contempt for the high principles of judicial equity which we avow as our excuse for the extraterritorial system—the "reign of law" which Justice Feetham declared to be the distinctive characteristic of Shanghai.
British judges, indeed, have at times had to animadvert emphatically on juries which were derelict in their duty in China. Judges seem to possess far more sense of responsibility than do jurymen out here, who sometimes show none whatsoever. What is the real task of an extraterritorial court—the shielding from justice of thugs and scoundrels of our own race, or the fair and honest application of law, and by it the protection of the good name of our courts of justice? Is it worth while, on the theory that "the Chinese will get too cheeky" if they are recognized as human beings with human rights and white men are punished for brutal offenses against them—is it worth while instead to extend actual protection and a coat of whitewash (which deceives no one) to some of the most callous, cruel, and vicious of our own race—men wholly lacking in human sympathy, in any sense of decency, in any feeling of mercy to an ill and helpless unfortunate of another race—men who lack even ordinary respect for human life? Do we really gain anything if we make our courts a shield and cloak for ruffians of our own race? Do we profit by bringing our administration of justice into contumely and contempt, making it a stench in the nostrils of all decent men of any nationality?
How many jurors out here ever think of such things?
Yours, etc.,
ANGLO-SAXON.
Shanghai, Feb. 12, 1935.
page_data.zh:
《上海晚邮报与水星报》，1936年2月14日，星期五 2 36

陪审团与正义

致编辑：

最近在此间发生的一起案件引发了关于陪审团审判的问题，这也凸显了此处英国法院与美国法院之间的根本差异。两家法院在很大程度上都遵循相同的英国法律。但是，在其中一家法院，被告可以像在祖国那样要求由陪审团进行审判，而在另一家法院，迄今为止，陪审团审判一直依惯例且始终被拒绝。

雷文（Raven）和布朗（Brown）因侵害其他美国人的罪行而被定罪。但也有一些案件涉及其他国籍人士，例如我们的东道主中国人。

当一名陪审员审理一起同胞被指控侵害其认为低于自己民族或群体的某国人之案件时，他心中究竟在想什么？在中国，有多少陪审员带着庄严而崇高的决心走进陪审席，誓要伸张正义，无论受害者是谁？有多少人真正尊重法律，真正尊重他们所服务的法庭的良好声誉？有多少人想到要在异国他乡树立自由与平等正义的典范，使其成为其他民族的光辉与楷模，并为此感到自豪？

陪审团审判是民主制度不可估量的成就之一。一个人要求由其同侪进行裁决的权利，是抵御官僚傲慢或压迫的宝贵屏障。但是，当像在中国这样，特殊条件使某些国籍群体处于特权阶级地位，凌驾于当地法律之上，仅受我们自身法律约束时，便涉及特殊的责任。其中首要的责任是维持公正无私的司法、法律面前的平等，以及法庭和陪审员表现出超越个人恩惠和个人偏见的姿态。唯有如此，唯有展现出比本地法庭更严格的正义与公平感，治外法权法庭才能在某种程度上证明其存在的合理性。

我想知道，在涉及本国国民对本地人犯下严重罪行的案件中，有多少陪审员曾考虑过此类事情。有多少人对我们自由的制度怀有自豪感，对这些制度抱有忠诚的本能？有多少人带着强烈的责任感走进陪审席——这种责任感要求他们在异国他乡、在数百万双眼睛的注视下，表明他们自己的法庭是正义的法庭、法律的法庭，其荣誉和美名必须由掌握案件裁决权的陪审员来维护？在这里，有多少陪审员受此类理解和原则的指导？

中国的治外法权历史揭示了一些有史以来对正义最可怕的歪曲。享有治外法权的外国人曾被指控犯下包括谋杀、强奸、武装抢劫、伪造在内的最严重罪行——这些指控往往有最完整且确凿的证据支持。但是，在我们的治外法权法庭上，从未有任何白人因此受到严厉惩罚。在此间的外国人中普遍存在一种观念，即如果因本国国民对中国人犯下严重罪行而予以惩罚，白人将失去威望。但是，相信罪犯应因此逃避正义的陪审员，无权坐在陪审席上。他仅仅因为接受陪审义务就构成了伪证，并玷污了法庭。他无意实行公正无私的司法；事实上他也无力做到。他与那些允许金钱决定其判决的法官一样腐朽、腐败和不诚实。

数百万中国人关注着治外法权法庭审理的每一宗外国人侵害中国人的严重罪行案件。他们好奇且急切地想看看，这些自称具有优越性和高标准的公平性的法庭，究竟如何实施我们引以为傲的“公正无私的司法”。而几乎在所有案件中，最终结果都是中国人对那些戏弄正义、包庇罪犯的外国法庭产生强烈的仇恨，以及对我们宣称作为治外法权制度借口的司法公平高尚原则——即费瑟姆（Feetham）法官所称的上海 distinctive characteristic（显著特征）“法治”——表示彻底的蔑视。

的确，英国法官有时不得不严厉批评在中国失职的陪审团。法官似乎比这里的陪审员拥有更强的责任感，后者有时完全缺乏责任感。治外法权法庭的真正任务是什么——是庇护我们种族中的暴徒和流氓免受正义制裁，还是公正诚实地适用法律，并以此维护我们司法法庭的美名？如果基于“如果承认中国人是拥有人权的人，并因白人对他们犯下残暴罪行而惩罚白人，中国人会变得太放肆”这一理论，转而为我们种族中一些最冷漠、残酷和恶毒的人提供实际保护和粉饰（这骗不了任何人）——这些人完全缺乏人类同情心、任何体面感或对另一种族病弱无助不幸者的任何怜悯之心——甚至缺乏对生命的基本尊重——这样做值得吗？如果我们使我们的法庭成为本族流氓的盾牌和掩护，我们真的能得到什么吗？通过使我们的司法行政陷入侮辱和蔑视，使其成为任何国籍的正派人士鼻中的恶臭，我们能获益吗？

在这里，有多少陪审员曾思考过此类事情？

此致，
盎格鲁-撒克逊人（ANGLO-SAXON）。
上海，1935年2月12日。

page_data.en:
The Shanghai Evening Post & Mercury, Saturday, February 15, 1936

The Jury System.
To the Editor:
Reading ANGLO-SAXON'S letter regarding juries and justice in your today's correspondence column compels me to say a few words on the recent acquittal of the Peter and Judd case. I am glad to see there are high-minded Anglo-Saxons who can see the effects of such an example of the jury system on us Chinese. I do not think it is necessary to be high-minded to see eye to eye with Anglo-Saxon To look at the matter in that light is merely to be sensible. Anglo-Saxon does not overtly mention the Peter and Judd case; but that is immaterial.
When I read in the morning papers about the verdict of Not Guilty and followed through the entire injunctions of the judge to the jury and came to the end, I threw up the paper and said: "Peter and Judd, go and throw a few more Chinese beggars into the Soochow creek! Why not? You are not even fined a cent or given a day at prison."
Now let us stop trying to be flip-pant, for it is out of no desire to say something for the sake of saying it that I write this. I wish merely to put down on record for the benefit of Europeans how the conduct of the entire case from the beginning to the end affected me as an ordinary Chinese, and especially as one who usually admires British justice, so far as any human justice on this earth can be admired at all. It isn't much, but it is something to be admired as far as we have got it, and it is certainly the basis for the claim to extra-territoriality.
My impressions during the conduct of the case were as follows. When the Police brought up the case for prosecution, I was agreeably shocked. I was distracted. I had known the western ideal of the law and justice, but on the other hand, I had been led by some recent cases which I need not mention here to believe that this law of justice does not apply in China. It seemed from the daily reports we were going to have justice. The idea of the British Crown prosecuting two British policemen for alleged murder of a poor Chinese beggar thrilled me as it should thrill any man. British justice was being put on trial and British justice seemed to be making a glorious record for itself. Inwardly, I said to myself: "If you handle justice fairly in a case between a national of your own and a poor, unknown Chinese beggar—damn it! you deserve extraterritoriality for another twenty years!"
Then when the prosecution pressed on with its evidence, I grew almost enthusiastic about the English, as I so often do among my own people. I remarked at home to my friends: "Look at the English! What we want in China is this kind of justice. A beggar is a beggar, and they are going to convict their own countrymen for throwing a poor beggar into the water. Well, they are English!" That was the height of apostrophe I was capable of.
Then came the end and the anticlimax, and all the judge's caution and repeated caution, and the carefully guided questions, and the interpretation of "malice" in legalistic phraseology and the question of "intentions."

The Shun Pao came out that morning with the caption with an adverbial conjunction which is untranslatable, ching. "The English Policemen ching were Acquitted." Ching resembles the German doch, but is much stronger in that it suggests something which could not have happened but which doch happened.
There was no further comment in the big or mosquito papers. We Chinese are accustomed to accepting this form of English justice as we accept the sun rising from the east.
I am here to record a fact, not to pass a judgment. The only moral I could point out is what Anglo-Saxon has already pointed out, viz., the inferiority of a system of justice which trusts the judgment of a few common, uneducated and easily influenced shop-keepers to a system which relies on the judgment of a hard-boiled, experienced judge.
Yours, etc.
A CHINESE.
Shanghai, February 14, 1936.

《上海晚邮报与水星报》，1936年2月15日，星期六

陪审团制度。

致编辑：

阅读今日贵报通信栏中“盎格鲁-撒克逊人”关于陪审团与正义的来信，促使我就彼得（Peter）和贾德（Judd）案最近的无罪判决说几句话。我很高兴看到有思想高尚的盎格鲁-撒克逊人能看到陪审团制度的这一范例对我们中国人的影响。我认为，不必思想高尚也能与盎格鲁-撒克逊人看法一致。从这个角度看待问题仅仅是明智之举。盎格鲁-撒克逊人并未明确提及彼得和贾德案；但这无关紧要。

当我在早报上看到“无罪”的判决，并通读了法官对陪审团的全部指示直到最后时，我把报纸扔掉，说道：“彼得和贾德，再去把几个中国乞丐扔进苏州河吧！为什么不呢？你们甚至连一分钱罚款都不用交，也不用坐一天牢。”

现在让我们停止轻浮的态度，因为我写这封信并非为了说话而说话。我只是希望记录下来，为了让欧洲人了解，整个案件从开始到结束的处理过程对我这个普通中国人，尤其是一个通常钦佩英国司法的人（只要世间任何人类司法值得钦佩的话），产生了怎样的影响。这虽然不多，但就我们所拥有的而言，它是值得钦佩的，并且无疑是主张治外法权的基础。

我在案件审理过程中的印象如下。当警方提出起诉时，我感到惊喜交加。我心神不定。我曾了解西方法律与正义的理想，但另一方面，最近的一些案件（此处无需提及）使我相信，这种正义之法并不适用于中国。从每日的报道来看，我们似乎即将得到正义。英国王室因两名英国警察涉嫌谋杀一名贫穷的中国乞丐而对其提起诉讼，这一想法令我激动不已，正如它应该令任何人激动一样。英国司法正在接受考验，而英国司法似乎正在为自己创造光荣的记录。我在心里对自己说：“如果你在自己国民与一个贫穷、无名的中国乞丐之间的案件中公正地处理正义——该死！你们配得上再拥有二十年的治外法权！”

随后，当控方继续出示证据时，我对英国人几乎变得热情起来，就像我经常在本国人中那样。我在家里对朋友们说：“看看英国人！我们在中国需要的就是这种正义。乞丐就是乞丐，而他们正要因将一名可怜乞丐扔进水里而定自己同胞的罪。嗯，他们是英国人！”那是我能做出的最高程度的赞叹。

接着迎来了结局和高潮的跌落，以及法官所有的谨慎和反复的警告，精心引导的提问，以法律术语对“恶意”的解释，以及关于“意图”的问题。

那天早上，《申报》刊出了一则标题，其中包含一个无法翻译的副词连词“竟”。“英国警察竟被宣告无罪。”“竟”类似于德语的 doch，但语气更强，因为它暗示了一件本不可能发生但却确实发生了的事情。

大型报纸或小报（mosquito papers）上没有进一步的评论。我们中国人习惯于接受这种形式的英国司法，就像我们接受太阳从东方升起一样。

我在此记录一个事实，而非做出评判。我能指出的唯一寓意是“盎格鲁-撒克逊人”已经指出的那一点，即：一个依赖少数普通、未受教育且易受影响的店主的判断的司法体系，劣于一个依赖经验丰富、老练法官的判断的体系。

此致，
一名中国人（A CHINESE）。
上海，1936年2月14日。

THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, FEBRUARY 12, 1936

THE ACQUITTAL
A seven-day trial of Sergeant E. W. Peters and Probationary Sergeant W. A. Judd on the charge of murdering a Chinese beggar, Mah Teh-piau, ended yesterday in H.M. Supreme Court with the acquittal of both prisoners. The verdict was given by the jury after a most patient and lucid exposition of the law and careful recapitulation of the evidence by the presiding Judge. The circumstances in which the deceased met his death have been recorded in sufficient detail to show that considerable room was left for surmise and even mystification. The Judge's function of expounding the law affecting the serious charge brought against the prisoners did not relieve the jury of their obligation to assess the facts, and, above all, to base their decision on the principle that the onus of proof lay upon the prosecution. The case was not clear-cut. Successful disentangement of the facts could be attempted only by those who, like the jury, were kept in close touch with the evidence and arguments on both sides during the whole of the trial. The decision must be taken to represent the jury's view that the prosecution had not fulfilled the conditions to which the Judge drew special attention in his reference to the important judgment of Viscount Sankey as Lord Chancellor in the House of Lords last May (Woolmington v. Director of Public Prosecutions):

Throughout the web of the English criminal law one golden thread is always to be seen, that it is the duty of the prosecution to prove the prisoner's guilt subject to matters as to the defence of insanity and subject also to any statutory exception.

Lord Sankey's dictum was introduced by a preceding passage in which he said

While the prosecution must prove the guilt of the prisoner, there is no such burden on the prisoner to prove his innocence and it is sufficient for him to raise a doubt as to his guilt; he is not bound to satisfy the jury of his innocence.

The defence counsel were able effectively to convince the jury that the facts produced in evidence gave rise to the doubt. Acquittal followed. The jury's verdict should be regarded in that light. The disclosures during the case called forth from the Bench serious comment on the state of affairs at the police station to which the prisoners were posted. Their acquittal does not establish the fact that their conduct as police officers was satisfactory. No doubt the police authorities, on whose initiative the prosecution was launched, will take suitable steps in that regard. The case incidentally draws attention once more to the complexity of the beggar problem. The policeman is expected to keep beggars off the streets. He is armed with inadequate powers. He is perforce reduced to the unsatisfactory device of depositing beggars in Chinese territory, whence return to the Settlement is only a question of time and opportunity. It would seem that some efforts should be made to establish a coordinated system with the aid of the Chinese authorities in order to bring these unfortunate derelicts within the scope of remedial influences, whether by punitive action or by some form of welfare work.

Commissioner of Police
Sir
J. M. Martin.
H. Gwernis
D. C. (Sp. Pr.)
（印：OFFICE OF COMMISSIONER OF POLICE SHANGHAI 13 FEB. 1936）

《字林西报》，1936年2月12日

无罪释放

警佐 E. W. Peters 和见习警佐 W. A. Judd 被控谋杀中国乞丐马德彪（Mah Teh-piau），为期七天的审判昨日在英王陛下最高法院结束，两名被告均被宣告无罪。在主审法官极其耐心且清晰地阐释法律并仔细重述证据之后，陪审团作出了裁决。关于死者死亡情形的记录已足够详细，表明其中留有相当大的推测甚至迷惑空间。法官阐释涉及对被告严重指控的法律之职能，并未免除陪审团评估事实的义务，尤其是未免除其基于“举证责任在于控方”这一原则作出决定的义务。本案并非一目了然。只有像陪审团那样在整个审判过程中密切关注双方证据和论点的人，才能尝试成功地厘清事实。必须认为，该决定代表了陪审团的观点，即控方未能满足法官在提及去年五月上议院大法官桑基子爵（Viscount Sankey）的重要判决（Woolmington v. Director of Public Prosecutions）时特别强调的条件：

贯穿英国刑法网络的一条金线始终可见，那就是控方有责任证明被告有罪，但有关精神错乱辩护的事项以及任何法定例外情况除外。

桑基勋爵的这句名言之前有一段引文，他说：

虽然控方必须证明被告有罪，但被告没有证明自己无罪的此类负担，他只需提出对其有罪的怀疑即可；他不必使陪审团确信其无罪。

辩护律师有效地说服了陪审团，使其相信所出示的证据事实引起了怀疑。随之而来的是无罪释放。陪审团的裁决应从这个角度来看待。案件审理过程中的披露引发了法庭对被告所属警察局状况的严肃评论。他们的无罪释放并不确立其作为警官的行为令人满意这一事实。毫无疑问，发起此次起诉的警方当局将就此采取适当措施。此案也再次引起人们对乞丐问题复杂性的关注。警察被期望将乞丐驱离街道。但他们手中的权力不足。他们被迫采取一种令人不满的做法，即将乞丐遣送至华界，而从那里返回租界只是时间和机会的问题。似乎应在中方当局的协助下努力建立一个协调体系，以便通过惩罚性行动或某种形式的福利工作，将这些不幸的流浪者纳入补救措施的范围之内。

警务处长
J. M. Martin 爵士
H. Gwernis
特别巡捕房副督察（D. C. (Sp. Pr.)）
（印：上海警务处长办公室 1936年2月13日）

D.7137

February 13, 1936. Morning translation.

China Evening News published the following comment on
February 12:-

BRITISH POLICEMEN FOUND "NOT GUILTY"

Two British policemen threw a sick Chinese
beggar into a creek. The beggar died. The policemen were
charged in the British Court./ In all 27 Chinese and
foreign witnesses were heard.

On February 11, the case ended. The judge
asked the jury whether the accused were guilty.

The jury (twelve British residents), after a
consulation lasting 40 minutes. declared that the British
policemen were "Not Guilty".

It was not surpirsing that applause came
from some of the people present in Court.

Was the sick Chinese beggar thrown into the
creek by the two British policemen or was he thrown upon
a beggar boat? The truth will never be known.

D.7137

1936年2月13日。晨译。

《China Evening News》于2月12日发表如下评论：

英国警察被判“无罪”

两名英国警察将一名生病的中国乞丐扔进一条小河。该乞丐死亡。这两名警察在英国法庭被起诉。共听取了27名中外证人的证词。

2月11日，案件审结。法官询问陪审团被告是否有罪。

陪审团（由十二名英国居民组成）经过40分钟的商议，宣布这两名英国警察“无罪”。

法庭上一些在场人士发出欢呼声，这并不令人惊讶。

这名生病的中国乞丐是被两名英国警察扔进小河的，还是被扔上了一艘乞丐船？真相将永远无人知晓。

February 11, 1936. Morning Translation.

Great Crystal (大晶报), a mosquito paper, published the following comment on February 9:-

REFLECTIONS OVER THE CASE AGAINST THE TWO FOREIGN POLICEMEN

At about 3 a.m. December 1, 1935, two foreign policemen (subjects of a civilized and progressive nation, Great Britain) whose duty is to protect the interests of residents, received information that a Chinese beggar was laying on Dixwell Road. They went there in motor car No. 8502 and subsequently threw the beggar into the Hongkew Creek. They did not know that the chauffeur, a Chinese named Doo Sun Fu (杜順福) and a Chinese policeman were paying close attention to their act or that a hawker named Sun Ching Sun (孫正生) later rescued the sick beggar from the creek or that two pedestrians named Nai Yih Sz (耐一士), male, and Chang Ah She (張阿喜), female, had also witnessed their action. However clever the arguments of the two policemen may be, the above evidence must be well established.

During the past few decades, Chinese people have been made special targets of insult. Friends returning from abroad say that when Americans and Europeans discovered that they were Chinese, they were looked upon with contempt. In Shanghai, when a Chinese farmer is knocked down and killed by a motor car owned by a foreigner, a compensation of $50 is paid. It seems that this is the standard price. Supposing that a Chinese knocks down and kills a dog belonging to a foreigner, it is a serious case. It was not surprising therefore that in the past, a board used to be exhibited in the parks prohibiting Chinese and dogs from entering the place. The value of the Chinese people is, in the eyes of foreigners, about the same as that of a dog and the value of a Chinese beggar is consequently much less.

The people of a backward civilized nation, China, are despised by people of progressive and civilized nations. Yet a sick beggar has been thrown into a creek by people of a progressive and civilized nation.

We are waiting to see how the kind Judge of the British Court will decide the case. Jesus Christ loved all people, poor and rich, in good health or in bad health. We know that the British people worship Jesus Christ.

China Times and other local newspapers:

SUPPRESSION OF UNAUTHORIZED LOTTERIES

Owing to the existence of a number of lotteries which have not been approved by the Government, the Ministry of Finance has ordered the various provincial governments to suppress all unauthorized lotteries and to order newspapers to refuse lottery advertisements and not to publish reports about these lotteries.

1936年2月11日。晨译。

小报《大晶报》于2月9日发表如下评论：

关于两名外籍警察案件的反思

1935年12月1日凌晨3时许，两名外籍警察（来自文明进步国家英国的臣民），其职责是保护居民利益，接到消息称有一名中国乞丐躺在狄思威路（Dixwell Road）。他们乘坐8502号汽车前往该处，随后将该乞丐扔进虹口港（Hongkew Creek）。他们不知道司机、一名名叫杜順福的中国人与一名中国巡捕正密切注视着他们的行为，也不知道一名名叫孫正生的小贩后来从河中救起了这名生病的乞丐，更不知道两名行人，男性耐一士（Nai Yih Sz）和女性張阿喜（Chang Ah She），也目睹了他们的行为。无论这两名警察的辩词多么巧妙，上述证据必须得到充分认定。

在过去几十年里，中国人一直是受侮辱的特殊目标。从海外归来的朋友说，当美国人和欧洲人发现他们是中国人时，便以轻蔑的眼光看待他们。在上海，当一名中国农民被外国人拥有的汽车撞倒致死时，仅支付50元赔偿金。这似乎是标准价格。假如一名中国人撞死了一条属于外国人的狗，那就是一起严重案件。因此，过去公园里曾竖立牌子禁止华人与狗入内，这并不令人惊讶。在外国人眼中，中国人的价值与狗大致相当，因此中国乞丐的价值就更低了。

落后文明国家中国的人民受到进步文明国家人民的鄙视。然而，一名生病的乞丐却被进步文明国家的人扔进了河里。

我们拭目以待英国法庭的仁慈法官将如何裁决此案。耶稣基督爱所有人，无论贫富，无论健康与否。我们知道英国人崇拜耶稣基督。

《China Times》及其他本地报纸：

取缔未经批准的彩票

由于存在许多未经政府批准的彩票，财政部已命令各省省政府取缔所有未经批准的彩票，并命令报纸拒绝刊登彩票广告，不发布有关这些彩票的报道。

THE SHANGHAI TIMES, TUESDAY, FEBRUARY 11, 1936

Evidence In Murder Trial
Summed Up Before Court
By Prosecution, Defence

Judd, Peters Testify On Their Own Behalf Regarding
Alleged Throwing Of Beggar Into The Creek;
Case Expected To Go To Jury To-day

MCDONALD MAKES COLOURFUL ADDRESS
IN DEFENCE OF POLICE OFFICERS

A gruelling examination of the two accused, and the summing-up addresses to the jury by counsel for the defence and by the prosecution, marked proceedings in H.B.M. Supreme Court yesterday before Judge A. G. Mossop, in the trial of Sergeant E. W. Peters and Probationary Sergeant W. A. Judd, S.M.P., on the charge of murdering a sick Chinese beggar by throwing him into Hongkew Creek on December 1. The case was adjourned at 5 p.m. until 9.30 this morning, when the judge will instruct the jury as to its duties before the jury goes out to find its verdict.

The examination of Sergeant Peters was concluded yesterday morning, after which Probationary Sergeant Judd took the stand on his own behalf.

In the afternoon Mr. Victor Priestwood, Crown Advocate, summed up the case for the prosecution, and was followed by Mr. Ranald McDonald, summing up for his client, Peters, and by Mr. H. A. Reeks for Judd. The courtroom was completely packed with spectators throughout the day, and large crowds gathered before both morning and afternoon sessions outside the locked doors long before the hour.

A number of friends of the accused, both police and civilians, was present in court, and the prisoners appeared quite cheerful.

Peters Under Fire

Sergeant Peters was questioned on events following the return to Kashing Road Police Station after the beggar had been disposed of, and on the motives in the testimony of various Chinese witnesses.

Mr. Priestwood—You have heard the driver say that he saw you throw the beggar into the creek with the aid of Judd. What motive has he for saying that?—None at all.

You say he was mistaken?—He was mistaken.

I put it to you that you threw that man into the water.—I did not.

You have also heard Sung Ching-sung say he saw two foreigners in uniform looking into the creek and shining a torch.—It probably was true.

When he says he went to the creek when the two foreigners had left and a man bobbing up and down in the water do you suggest that he is telling an untruth?—I couldn't say.

When you hear him and his neighbours say that the nearest boat was not a beggar boat but an empty cargo firewood boat, what motive do you ascribe to that?—It was a beggar boat.

That's not my question.

Mr. McDonald—It's his answer.

Judd Takes Stand

Peters was followed to the stand by Judd at about 10.30. He told his story, led by Mr. Reeks. He was born in England, was 26 years old, and his parents now live at Duncaster, Yorkshire, his birthplace. He joined the army, served in the Duke of Wellington's Regiment for seven years in England, Gibraltar and China. He was transferred to reserve May 18, 1933, and three days later he signed up with the Shanghai Municipal Police. He said that he had a very good character rating on his army discharge. The discharge had been left at the Ward Road Gaol.

He spent two months in training depot and was sent to West Hongkew Station. Later he was at Central and then in the reserve unit. On November 25, 1935, he was assigned to Kashing Road Station and went on night patrol duty. He was engaged in that duty on the night of November 30—December 1. He came into the charge room for coffee at 2.30 a.m. He was supposed to have coffee time from 3 a.m. to 3.20 a.m. Peters told him to get warm and then go on patrol again. About that time a telephone call came in regarding a sick beggar. Asked if he had seen sick beggars before he said that he had, many times. "Beggars run from policemen," he said. "If they don't run they are probably sick."

"Suppose He Is Sick"

Continuing, Judd said that he went with Peters because he was not certain of the way. They proceeded to Point and Sinkeipang Roads.

"We saw a male Chinese beggar lying by a wall. I spoke to him and told him to get up. He didn't answer. Peters said: 'I suppose he is sick. We had better take him to hospital.' We lifted him to his feet and walked with him across to the car and put him on the running board. Peters was standing on the running board.

"While going to the hospital I heard Peters calling in Chinese to the beggar not to move. He called several times. When we got to what I later learned was Nanzing Road—I didn't know then that it was Nanzing Road—Peters told the chauffeur to stop.

"He said, 'This man is not very sick. He has nearly knocked me off the car two or three times. They won't admit him to hospital now. We had best put him on one of these beggar boats in the creek.'"

They drove along to Fearon Road. "We both saw a beggar boat a bit to the rear of the car, and we then went back to the car. The beggar by then was almost sitting up. We walked with him over to the side of the creek opposite the boat and put him down. We helped him under the lower rail. Before we helped him Peters pointed to the boat below and the man nodded his head. We got over the top rail and lowered him onto the boat. We saw that he was on the boat. Then we went back to the car. I got in first, and the dog jumped over from the front seat to the rear."

On the night of December 2, Judd continued, he was summoned to hear a report read by Captain Kennedy of a charge to be placed against him. "I said then, 'That is a lie. We didn't do that.'"

Cross-Examined

Here Mr. Priestwood began cross-examination. Judd admitted that the weather was quite cold. He said that he could have found the place where the beggar was lying as quickly without the aid of Peters. He said that the beggar was "grunting," not "moaning." The man was not unable to walk, but scuffled along to the car. They both wanted to carry the man on the running board. Asked why the customary procedure—calling an ambulance—was not followed, Judd said that he had used raiding vans and ambulances in such cases. "But the ambulance is a nice clean ambulance and those beggars are very dirty."

When he was asked if the dog jumped out of the car, Judd said yes. "Incidentally, he chased a cat along the road."

When it was suggested that his written statement as to seeing a beggar boat when they were crossing East Hanbury Road bridge was not correct, he admitted it. He said that he had supposed Peters had seen one.

He explained that he had asked for time to think over his statement because he thought the charge of throwing a beggar into the creek was a trap to get a confession out of him about crossing the bridge into the Hongkew police district, which was against regulations.

He denied any knowledge of the allegation that Peters had reported for duty in the charge room late on that night.

Summing-up Begun

This practically concluded the morning session. The Court sat again at 2.15 p.m. when Mr. Priestwood summed up the case for the prosecution in a 45-minute address to the jury.

After thanking the jury for their patience and understanding, he submitted that the prosecution had proved its case and had called up through witnesses all facts material on which the jury could form its judgment. It had been proved beyond all reasonable doubt that Peters and Judd were of sound memory and discretion on the night in question, and that they did without provocation cause, intentionally, the death of a person under the King's peace.

Mr. Priestwood went on to say that there was only one conclusion. Peters was in the charge room after coming in two and a half hours late, and on arrival he proceeded to break all the rules and regulations he possibly could, and disrupted station routine by calling on Sergeant Makovetsky to take charge, who was present when Peters arrived. 谋杀案审判证据
控辩双方总结陈词

贾德（Judd）、彼得斯（Peters）就涉嫌将乞丐扔入河浜一事自行作证；
案件预计今日提交陪审团裁决

麦克唐纳为警务人员辩护发表精彩演说

昨日，在英国驻华最高法院（H.B.M. Supreme Court），由莫索普（A. G. Mossop）法官主持，对上海公共租界工部局警务处（S.M.P.）警佐E. W. 彼得斯和试用警佐W. A. 贾德被控于12月1日将一名患病中国乞丐扔进虹口河浜致其死亡一案进行审理。庭审以对两名被告的严苛讯问，以及辩方和控方律师向陪审团所作的总结陈词为标志。下午5时休庭，直至今天上午9时30分复庭，届时法官将在陪审团退庭商议裁决前，向其指示职责。

彼得斯警佐的讯问于昨日上午结束，随后试用警佐贾德出庭为自己作证。

下午，王室检察官维克多·普里斯特伍德（Victor Priestwood）先生代表控方作总结陈词，随后是代表其当事人彼得斯的拉纳德·麦克唐纳（Ranald McDonald）先生，以及代表贾德的H. A. 里克斯（H. A. Reeks）先生。全天法庭内座无虚席，旁听者众多；在上午和下午开庭前很久，紧闭的大门外就已聚集了大量人群。

多名被告的朋友，包括警务人员和平民，出席了庭审，被告们显得相当轻松愉快。

彼得斯受到质询

彼得斯警佐就处置乞丐后返回嘉兴路警察局期间发生的事件，以及多位中国证人证词中的动机问题接受了质询。

普里斯特伍德先生——你听到司机说，他看见你在贾德的协助下将乞丐扔进河浜。他这么说有什么动机？——完全没有。

你说他搞错了？——他搞错了。

我向你指出，是你把那个人扔进水里的。——我没有。

你还听到宋景松（Sung Ching-sung，音译）说，他看见两名身穿制服的外国人正在往河浜里看，并打着手电筒。——这可能是真的。

当他说在那两名外国人离开后，他走到河浜边，看到一个人头在水中起伏时，你认为他在撒谎吗？——我说不上来。

当你听到他和他的邻居说，最近的一艘船不是乞丐船，而是一艘空的运柴货船时，你认为这背后有什么动机？——那就是一艘乞丐船。

那不是我的问题。

麦克唐纳先生——那是他的回答。

贾德出庭作证

大约10时30分，贾德继彼得斯之后出庭作证。他在里克斯先生的引导下陈述了自己的经历。他出生于英国，现年26岁，父母目前居住在他的出生地约克郡邓卡斯特（Duncaster）。他参军后，在威灵顿公爵团服役七年，驻防地点包括英国、直布罗陀和中国。他于1933年5月18日转入预备役，三天后签约加入上海公共租界工部局警务处。他说，他的军队退伍鉴定评级很好。退伍文件留在了华德路监狱。

他在训练所度过了两个月，随后被派往虹口西区警局。后来他在中央警局任职，之后又在预备队服役。1935年11月25日，他被分配至嘉兴路警局，并开始执行夜间巡逻任务。11月30日至12月1日夜间，他正在执行该任务。凌晨2时30分，他进入值班室喝咖啡。按规定，他的咖啡时间是凌晨3时至3时20分。彼得斯让他去暖和一下，然后继续巡逻。就在那时，接到一个关于一名患病乞丐的电话。当被问及以前是否见过患病的乞丐时，他说见过，很多次。“乞丐见到警察就跑，”他说，“如果不跑，那可能就是病了。”

“假设他病了”

贾德继续说道，他之所以和彼得斯一起去，是因为他不认得路。他们前往百老汇路（Point Road）和新嘉坡路（Sinkeipang Road，音译）。

“我们看见一名中国男乞丐躺在墙边。我跟他说话，叫他起来。他没有回应。彼得斯说：‘我想他是病了。我们最好把他送到医院去。’我们将他扶起，搀扶着他走到汽车旁，让他站在踏脚板上。彼得斯也站在踏脚板上。

“在去医院的路上，我听到彼得斯用中文喊叫，让乞丐不要动。他喊了好几次。当我们到达后来我得知是南京路的地方时——我当时不知道那是南京路——彼得斯告诉司机停车。

“他说，‘这个人病得不重。他在车上差点把我撞下来两三次。现在医院不会收他的。我们最好把他放在河浜里的一艘乞丐船上。’

“他们沿着道路开往斐伦路（Fearon Road）。‘我们都看到车后方不远处有一艘乞丐船，于是我们折返回到车旁。那时乞丐几乎已经坐起来了。我们搀扶着他走到河浜边，正对着那艘船的位置，把他放下。我们帮他从下栏杆下面钻过去。在帮忙之前，彼得斯指了指下面的船，那人点了点头。我们翻过上栏杆，将他放到船上。我们看到他已在船上。然后我们回到车旁。我先上了车，狗从前座跳到了后座。’”

贾德继续说，12月2日晚上，他被传唤去听肯尼迪（Kennedy）上尉宣读一份针对他的指控报告。“我当时说，‘那是谎言。我们没有那样做。’”

交叉盘问

此时，普里斯特伍德先生开始交叉盘问。贾德承认天气相当寒冷。他说，即使没有彼得斯的帮助，他也能同样快地找到乞丐躺卧的地方。他说乞丐是在“哼哼”，而不是“呻吟”。那人并非不能行走，而是拖着脚步走向汽车。两人都想把那人放在踏脚板上。当被问及为何不遵循常规程序——呼叫救护车时，贾德说他在此类情况下曾使用过突击车和救护车。“但救护车是干净舒适的，而那些乞丐非常脏。”

当被问及狗是否从车里跳出来时，贾德说是的。“顺便说一句，它沿着路追了一只猫。”

当有人指出他关于在穿过东汉伯雷路（East Hanbury Road）桥时看到一艘乞丐船的书面陈述不正确时，他予以承认。他说他当时以为彼得斯看到了一艘船。

他解释说，他要求时间考虑自己的陈述，是因为他认为将乞丐扔进河浜的指控是一个陷阱，旨在诱使他承认违规越过桥梁进入虹口警区，这是违反规定的行为。

他否认知晓有关彼得斯当晚迟归值班室报到的指控。

开始总结陈词

上午的庭审至此基本结束。法庭于下午2时15分再次开庭，普里斯特伍德先生用45分钟的时间向陪审团作了控方总结陈词。

在感谢陪审团的耐心和理解后，他提出控方已证明其案情，并通过证人传唤了所有有助于陪审团形成判断的重要事实。已无可置疑地证明，彼得斯和贾德在事发当晚神志清醒、具有判断力，且他们在毫无挑衅的情况下，故意导致了一名处于国王治下和平状态的人死亡。

普里斯特伍德先生接着说，结论只有一个。彼得斯迟到两个半小时后才进入值班室，一到那里他就着手打破所有可能打破的规章制度，并通过叫来当时在场的马科维茨基（Makovetsky，音译）警佐负责指挥，扰乱了警局的日常运作。收到一条电话留言，并在贾德在场的情况下转达给彼得斯，该留言称有一名乞丐躺在……

（印：档案 1936年2月11日）

"Beyond all possible or reason-
able doubt it has been proved
that there was a beggar, very
ill, at that place," Mr. Priestwood
continued. "Peters then did
assist Judd, and vice versa, and
picked up and dragged the man
to the car and put him on the
running board and fender, which
was against the usual method of
procedure in such cases—that is,
calling an ambulance."

A Painful Thing

They then went along a route
directed by Peters to Nanzing
Road, Mr. Priestwood went on,
and afterward the car turned
back to Fearon Road to a point
halfway between Yuhang and
Haining Roads.

"Although the witness Sung
Ching-sang may be a hawker or
even a pimp as has been sug-
gested, he has entered a British
court and given evidence on oath.
The fact that the chauffeur is a
member of the Shanghai Muni-
cipal Police is not an inducement
to enter this court and give such
evidence on oath. Gentlemen, you
can rely on their evidence. . . . It
must have been a very painful
thing for the chauffeur to make
such a report against his superior
officers, as he did in his state-
ment, and when he told you that
he did see Peters take the man
off the car running board and
with Judd throw the man over
the railing, he was speaking the
truth. When Sung said that he
stood outside his door and saw a
car—the licence number of which
he took because he can read num-
bers—and saw two foreigners in
uniform looking down into the
creek, he was also speaking the
truth.

"Gentlemen, you will realize
from your own knowledge that
Chinese can be very curious about
inconsequential events; you have
seen crowds congregate many
times for practically no reason at
all. This hawker was curious
when he saw the foreigners there,
late at night, looking into the
creek and using a flashlight. He
went across and looked and saw
a man in the water.

False Entry Made

"If there had been a beggar
boat near-by, it would not have
been necessary, as he did, for
Sung to cry out loudly 'Save life,
save life!' The nearest boat was
some distance north. If it had
been suggested then to Sung
that he would be put up to this
story he would not have cried out
—to be contradicted later in
court."

Peters returned to the station,
Mr. Priestwood continued, and
there made a false entry in the
book, though it was not his busi-
ness to write such an entry in.
He did this because he wished to
cover up his movements and to
hide the fact that he had thrown
the beggar into the creek.

Peters was later cautioned by
Captain Kennedy, Mr. Priestwood
said. He was told of the allega-
tions, and he then made another
false statement, deliberately.
Peters consulted Judd as to what
the entry in the book should be.
After Peters made his state-
ment, he had decided to amend it,
realizing the seriousness of the
charge.

"Peters has proved that he
lied," Mr. Priestwood declared,
"lying to save his skin!"

Knew His Way

Regarding Judd's part in the
affair, Mr. Priestwood said, Judd
came off duty for coffee at the
wrong time. Sergeant Makovetsky
was in the charge room then.
Judd heard the clerk give the tele-
phone message about the beggar,
and he said: "That must be the man
I saw." Judd did know his way
about the district, though he had
denied it, and he realized that he
had seen the same beggar. If Judd
hadn't known his way around, why
did Peters tell Judd to go, rather
than Makovetsky?

Judd went with Peters and
helped put the man on the car and
they drove over East Hanbury
Road bridge, where Judd later said
he saw a beggar boat in the creek.
As a matter of fact, it was
impossible to see a beggar boat
in the creek from that bridge or
from Fearon Road from the car.

The testimony of the hawker
and the chauffeur were also against
Judd as well as Peters, Mr. Priest-
wood declared, for otherwise they
would not have come into the court
and by perjury attempt to convict
the men of murder.

Wished To Cover Up

At 7 o'clock at the home, and was at-
tended by a large and representa-
tive gathering. "Lead, Kindly
Light" was sung as an opening
hymn, this being especially re-
quested by Mrs. Corbett herself.
Following a prayer by the Rev.
Herbert Taylor of the China In-
land Mission, another hymn, "The
Sands of Time Are Sinking," was
sung, after which the Rev. J. Ed-
ward Kidder of the Presbyterian
Mission read Scripture passages
consisting of Psalm 90, I Cor. 15:-
51-58, and II Tim. 4:5-8. "Going
Home" by Dvorak, sung as a duet
by Mrs. F. E. Dilley and Mrs. D.
F. R. McMullan, seemed most fit-
ting and appropriate, and struck
a tender chord in the hearts of
all present. After a prayer by the
Rev. D. A. Irwin of the Presby-
terian Mission, the Rev. G. F.
Browne of the same Mission made
a short address based on Ps.17.1b
and Rev. 22:4. He spoke of Mrs.
Corbett's stately bearing, her

Mr. Priestwood could not believe
that the reasons Peters gave for
writing the entry in the book were
good reasons. He, Mr. Priestwood,
asked many questions of Peters
while the latter was in the witness
box and had asked them fast be-
cause otherwise Peters would have
had time to think up other lies.

Judd's defence, Mr. Priestwood
declared, was the same story. The
man was not telling the truth.
The beggar found by the ambul-
ance was the same beggar taken
by Peters and Judd to Fearon
Road. He was the same beggar
who died in the hospital of double
pneumonia six days later. That
man had caught pneumonia some
four to five-and-a-half days before,
as proved in the autopsy. It was
the new pneumonia that assisted
in the death.

Mr. Priestwood again quoted the
law in defining the term murder,
to the effect that those who do
something to sick persons, or
neglect them, thereby causing
their death, are guilty of murder.
His conclusion was that both the
prisoners in the dock were guilty
of that crime.

Mr. McDonald's Contentions

The case for the prosecution
having been summed up, Mr.
McDonald rose to sum up the
defence for Peters. He said, open-
ing, that he felt a great sense of
responsibility. His client was on
trial for his life. He was a young
man and his life meant much to
him. It probably meant more to

If the prosecution was correct,
Peters had committed murder.
There could be no half-way meas-
ures in this, it was either murder
or it was not.

"If you have any doubt on any
one point in the prosecution of
this case, then you must find my
client not guilty."

Mr. McDonald warned the jury
not to take into any account any
local newspaper accounts of the
trial, and said he had seen an
account of some evidence, publish-
ed in a local paper, that had been
excluded as evidence from the
court.

"I have had much assistance
from my learned friend, the Crown
Advocate," he said. He added that
there had been some differences
between prosecution and defence,
but "a little heat" was general in
such matters. He had chiefly
objected to leading questions. The
Court was merely trying to con-
form with the finest traditions of
a system of justice that any race
of human beings has ever seen in
this world.

The witnesses from St. Luke's
hospital, Mr. McDonald said, had
been very fair. An hydrographer,

Myrtle Ivanoff, 15, left her
Island, to go to school in Scot-
land about civilization except the ab-
ove pictured doing some home work.
Mrs. Springer, former government
official, came to the United States.

Chefoo, then told something of the
service which was held last week
in the Shanghai Community
Church. He mentioned his own
growing appreciation of how wide-
ly Mrs. Corbett was known, and
how she numbered her friends
from every station and walk of
life.

After another hymn, "Hark,
Hark, My Soul," the Rev. A. J.
Lutley, of the Church of England
led in prayer, which was followed
by the benediction by the Rev.
Walton Moore, of the Baptist Mis-
sion. Mrs. Dilley played Chopin's
"Funeral March" after which the
congregation moved out to form
the procession to the near-by
cemetery. As the casket was borne
from the house the church
bell began to toll its seven,
seven strokes, indicating the age
of the deceased.

Pall-Bearers

Because of Mrs. Corbett's many
years of service among the Chin-
ese by whom she was dearly loved,
they especially requested the
privilege of assisting in carrying
her body to the grave. The pall-
bearers were Rev. D. A. Lewis,
Rev. J. W. Moore, Messrs. A. L.
Grubb, Albert Rouse, R. A. Lan-
ning, D. F. Murray, Sen Hai-
Li Loa, Wang Ching-wu, Yu Yi-
dzai, Dr. Chang Feng-ch'ing, and
one other Chinese. Honorary pall-
bearers were Dr. F. E. Dilley, Dr.
H. Bryan, Dr. F. H. Judd, Dr.
Malcolm, Rev. Li Si-hoa, and Rev.
Liu Dzi-tang. The procession was
led by the Rev. G. F. Browne and
the Rev. Cheng Ching-dao.

At the grave, "Lead Kindly
Light" was sung in Chinese, fol-
lowed by prayer by the Rev. H.
Ke-li. The committal service in
English was followed by the Lord's

“已经毫无疑问且合理地证明，当时那里确实有一名病重的乞丐，”普里斯特伍德先生继续说道。“彼得斯随后协助了贾德，反之亦然，他们将那人抬起并拖到汽车旁，把他放在踏脚板和挡泥板上，这违背了此类案件通常的处理程序——即呼叫救护车。”

一件痛苦的事

他们随后沿着彼得斯指示的路线前往南京路，普里斯特伍德先生接着说，之后汽车又折返至斐伦路（Fearon Road），停在余杭路与海宁路之间的中点。

“虽然证人宋景三（Sung Ching-sang，音译）可能像有人暗示的那样是个小贩，甚至是皮条客，但他已进入英国法庭并在宣誓后作证。司机身为上海公共租界工部局警务处的一员，这一事实并非诱使他进入本庭并作此宣誓证词的动力。诸位，你们可以信赖他们的证词……对于司机来说，像他在陈述中所做的那样，指控他的上级官员，必定是一件非常痛苦的事情；当他说他确实看到彼得斯将那人从汽车踏脚板上弄下来，并与贾德一起将那人扔过栏杆时，他讲的是真话。当宋某说他站在自家门外，看到一辆汽车——因为他识数所以记下了车牌号——并看到两名身穿制服的外国人正低头向浜里张望时，他讲的也是真话。

“诸位，根据你们自身的了解，你们会意识到中国人对无关紧要的小事往往非常好奇；你们曾多次看到人群几乎毫无理由地聚集。这名小贩在深夜看到那些外国人在那里用手电筒向浜里张望，感到很好奇。他走过去查看，看到水里有一个人。

伪造记录

“如果附近有一艘丐船，宋某就不必像他那样大声呼喊‘救命，救命！’最近的船只在北边一段距离之外。如果当时有人暗示宋某编造这个故事，他就不会大声呼喊——以免日后在法庭上被驳斥。”

普里斯特伍德先生继续说，彼得斯回到巡捕房后，在登记簿上做了虚假记录，尽管记录此类事项并非他的职责。他这样做是因为他想掩盖自己的行踪，并隐瞒他将乞丐扔进浜里的事实。

普里斯特伍德先生说，彼得斯后来受到肯尼迪警司的告诫。有人向他告知了相关指控，随后他故意作了另一份虚假陈述。彼得斯就登记簿上应如何记录一事咨询了贾德。彼得斯作出陈述后，意识到指控的严重性，决定对其进行修改。

“彼得斯已证明他撒了谎，”普里斯特伍德先生宣称，“撒谎是为了保全自己！”

熟悉地形

关于贾德在此事中的角色，普里斯特伍德先生说，贾德在错误的时间下班去喝咖啡。当时马科维茨基（Makovetsky，音译）巡长正在值班室。贾德听到办事员传达关于乞丐的电话留言，他说：“那一定是我看到的那个人。”贾德确实熟悉该地区的地形，尽管他予以否认，而且他意识到自己看到的是同一个乞丐。如果贾德不熟悉地形，为什么彼得斯让贾德去，而不是让马科维茨基去？

贾德随彼得斯一同前往，并帮忙将那人抬上车，他们驾车驶过东汉伯里路（East Hanbury Road）桥，贾德后来称他在那里看到浜里有一艘丐船。事实上，从那座桥上或从斐伦路上的汽车里，根本不可能看到浜里的丐船。

普里斯特伍德先生宣称，小贩和司机的证词不仅对彼得斯不利，对贾德也不利，否则他们就不会来到法庭，并通过伪证试图给这些人定谋杀罪。

企图掩盖

普里斯特伍德先生无法相信彼得斯给出的在登记簿上做记录的理由是正当的。普里斯特伍德先生在彼得斯站在证人席上时向他提出了许多问题，并且提问速度很快，因为否则彼得斯就有时间编造其他谎言。

普里斯特伍德先生宣称，贾德的辩护也是同样的说辞。此人没有讲真话。由救护车发现的乞丐，就是被彼得斯和贾德带到斐伦路的那个乞丐。他就是六天后在医院死于双叶肺炎的同一个乞丐。尸检证明，那人在死前四到五天半左右患上了肺炎。正是新发的肺炎导致了死亡。

普里斯特伍德先生再次引用法律对谋杀一词的定义，大意是：那些对病人采取某种行动或忽视他们，从而导致其死亡的人，犯有谋杀罪。他的结论是，被告席上的两名囚犯均犯有此罪。

麦克唐纳先生的论点

控方总结陈词结束后，麦克唐纳先生起身为彼得斯进行辩护总结。他开场时表示，他深感责任重大。他的当事人正面临生死审判。他是一个年轻人，生命对他意义重大。这可能更意味着

如果控方是正确的，那么彼得斯就犯了谋杀罪。在此事上没有中间地带，要么是谋杀，要么不是。

“如果你们对本案控方的任何一点存有疑虑，那么你们必须裁定我的当事人无罪。”

麦克唐纳先生警告陪审团不要考虑任何当地报纸对审判的报道，并说他看到当地报纸刊登了一些已被法庭排除在证据之外的证词报道。

“我从我的博学朋友，即皇家检察官那里得到了很多帮助，”他说。他补充说，控辩双方存在一些分歧，但在此类事务中“一点火气”是很常见的。他主要反对诱导性提问。法庭 merely 试图遵循任何人类种族在这个世界上所见过的最完善的司法体系的传统。

February 8, 1936. Morning Translation.

The "Holmes"(福尔摩斯) published the following comment on February 7 :-

DELIBERATE MANSLAUGHTER

Chinese people use to regard the Foreign Settlements as a place of refuge and peace. One is not only glad at heart but is proud to be in a position to reside in the Foreign Settlements under the protection of lordly foreigners.
Yet, are the Foreign Settlements really a place of refuge and peace? This may be true for rich and influential persons, but for the lower class Chinese, they are by no means a place of refuge but a hell on earth.
About a month or two ago, a sick beggar was found lying on Hung Jao(虹桥) bridge by two foreign lordly policemen who pushed him into a creek, thereby sending him to the "western heaven". This murder would not have been discovered had it not been witnessed and made public by several lower class Chinese. Thus, the S.M.C. had to take up the matter while the British Supreme Court had to charge the two policemen. No matter what the verdict of the Court may be, the fact remains that the death of the sick beggar had been caused by the "devils of hell".
The other day while a painter named Sung Tsung Hwa(孙振华) was passing by Chiu Ching Lee(赵锦里) on his way home on the second day of this month (?), it so happened that at the time a lawless character snatched a hand-bag from a girl student who immediately shouted out "Robbers". Two Chinese policemen heard the cry and gave chase. Taking the painter for the robber, they fired at him four shots in succession and killed him. The Shanghai Chamber of Commerce has sent to the S.M.C. a letter relating to this case requesting it to punish the two Chinese policemen for deliberate manslaughter. Whether or not the letter will have any effect one cannot say, but of one thing one may be certain, namely, the death of the painter is a fact. Supposing the painter was dressed in fur and was riding in a motor car, would he have been mistaken by the lordly policemen as a robber and shot dead?
Are the Foreign Settlements a place of refuge and peace? Or are they a hell on earth?

1936年2月8日。晨间译稿。

《福尔摩斯》报于2月7日发表如下评论：—

故意杀人

中国人历来将外国租界视为避难与和平之地。人们不仅心中欢喜，而且为能在尊贵的外国人的保护下居住于外国租界而感到自豪。
然而，外国租界真的是避难与和平之地吗？这对富有且有影响力的人来说或许如此，但对于下层中国民众而言，这里绝非避难所，而是人间地狱。
大约一两个月前，两名外国尊贵的警察发现一名生病的乞丐躺在虹桥上，便将他推入一条浜中，从而送他去了“西天”。若非几名下层中国人目睹并公开此事，这起谋杀案本不会被发现。因此，工部局不得不介入此事，而英国最高法院也不得不起诉这两名警察。无论法院判决如何，事实依然是，这名生病乞丐的死是由“地狱魔鬼”造成的。
日前，一名名叫孙振华的油漆工在本月2日（？）回家途中经过赵锦里时，恰逢一名不法之徒从一名女学生手中抢走手提包，该女生立即高呼“抓强盗”。两名中国警察听到呼救声并展开追捕。他们将油漆工误认为强盗，连续向他开了四枪，将其打死。上海总商会已就此案致函工部局，要求惩处这两名故意杀人的中国警察。这封信是否会产生效果尚不可知，但有一点可以肯定，即油漆工之死是事实。假如这名油漆工身穿皮草，乘坐汽车，那些尊贵的警察还会将他误认为强盗并开枪打死吗？
外国租界是避难与和平之地吗？还是人间地狱？

《China Evening News》于2月7日发表如下社论：—

关于外国警察将乞丐扔进浜里的案件

两名外国警察用汽车运走了一名被发现躺在地上的生病乞丐。来到一条浜边时，警官将他扔了进去。这种行为极不恰当。但是，上海的外国租界构成一个特殊的世界，居住在租界的中国人受到特殊对待。外国居民，尤其是警察，特别是外国租界的外国警察，以特殊的眼光看待中国人。因此，在这起乞丐案件中，

February 8, 1936. Morning Translation.

the foreign Police officers regarded him in a more special
light.
The two foreign policemen are being charged
in the British Court and some 30 witnesses have been heard.
On February 5, the chauffeur who drove the motor car
conveying the beggar to the creek was questioned and on
February 6 the hawker who rescued the beggar out of the water
after he had been thrown into the creek was interrogated.
It is said that more witnesses will be heard and that the
case will be concluded next Tuesday or Wednesday. This
shows how much attention the British authorities are
paying to the case. The lawyers retained by the two
foreign policemen are very fierce. On February 5, they
questioned the chauffeur for over 6 hours and on the following
day, the hawker was questioned. Thus the driver and the
hawker may fall into traps laid by the lawyers.
It has now been established that the sick beggar
was not removed to a hospital but to the side of a creek;
it has also been established that the beggar was thrown
into the creek. The point as to whether the beggar fell
on a beggar boat when he was thrown into the creek or
whether the beggar was thrown into the creek itself has
not yet been ascertained. If the beggar fell on the
beggar boat, then the statement made by the hawker is false.
For this reason the lawyers for the defence of the two
foreign policemen on February 6 did their best to show that
the hawker was a notorious character.
We do not desire to comment on the case while
it is sub judice. This case has drawn our attention to
Police affairs in the Foreign Settlements and we take
this opportunity to make the following observations:-
One can notice on the streets at any time arbitrary
acts committed by the lordly policemen who display their
majesty to ricsha coolies, hawkers, prostitutes and beggars.
Of course, in the eyes of the authorities of the Foreign
Settlements, these people are so much filth, but however
dirty they may be, they are human beings, although they
are not treated as such. Licences of ricshas are taken
away, their cushions are seized, the coolies kneel on the
road begging the policemen for their return. Stalls of
hawkers are overturned with kicks and the wares scattered
about on the ground and the hawkers are taken to the Police
Station. In cold weather, prostitutes hurriedly run away
at the approach of policemen. They are detained in prison
if arrested. As to the treatment of beggars, the present
case is a good example and needs no further comment.
These men and women represent the lower section
of the community. Whatever may be the condition of the
Settlement, its foundations are based on this lower section
of the community. Yet these people are being given such
treatment!
We may not hope that this small case will wake
the authorities of the Foreign Settlements to their senses,
but we do hope that it will serve as a clear warning to
Chinese residents in the Settlements.

外籍警员对他另眼相看。
两名外籍警察正在英国法院受审，已有约30名证人出庭作证。2月5日，驾驶将乞丐运送至河浜的汽车司机接受了讯问；2月6日，在乞丐被抛入河浜后将其从水中救起的小贩也接受了审讯。据悉还将听取更多证人的证词，案件将于下周二或周三结案。这表明英国当局对该案给予了高度关注。两名外籍警察聘请的律师非常厉害。2月5日，他们盘问司机长达6个多小时，次日又盘问了小贩。因此，司机和小贩可能会落入律师设下的陷阱。
现已查明，这名生病的乞丐并未被送往医院，而是被带至河浜边；也已查明，该乞丐被抛入了河浜。至于乞丐被抛入河浜时是落在了一艘丐船上，还是直接被抛入河浜水中，这一点尚未查清。如果乞丐是落在了丐船上，那么小贩的陈述就是虚假的。出于这个原因，两名外籍警察的辩护律师在2月6日极力证明该小贩是个声名狼藉的人物。
我们不愿在案件审理期间对此案发表评论。此案引起了我们对租界警务事务的关注，我们借此机会提出以下意见：
人们随时可以在街头看到那些傲慢的警察对人力车夫、小贩、妓女和乞丐摆出威风凛凛的姿态，肆意妄为。当然，在租界当局眼中，这些人不过是污秽之物，但无论他们多么肮脏，他们毕竟是人，尽管并未被当作人对待。人力车的执照被吊销，坐垫被没收，车夫们跪在路上乞求警察归还。小贩的摊位被踢翻，货物散落一地，小贩则被带到警察局。天气寒冷时，妓女一见警察靠近便匆忙逃散。若被捕，她们会被关进监狱。至于对待乞丐的方式，本案即是一个很好的例子，无需多言。
这些男女代表着社会的底层。无论租界的状况如何，其基础都建立在这一社会底层之上。然而，这些人却遭受着如此待遇！
我们不敢指望这起小案能让租界当局清醒过来，但我们希望它能给租界内的中国居民一个明确的警示。

THE SHANGHAI TIMES, SATURDAY, FEBRUARY 8, 1936

Witnesses Piling Up In
Prosecution Of Beggar
Case At Supreme Court

Inspector Bennett And Dr. Tucker Among Important
Witnesses On Stand During Lengthy Session;
Case Cannot Be Concluded By This Noon

COMIC RELIEF GIVEN BY INTERJECTIONS,
BICKERING; STATEMENTS ARE READ

A bewildering array of prosecution witnesses followed one another in close succession in the witness stand yesterday during continuation of the trial of Sergeant E. W. Peters and Probationary Sergeant W. A. Judd, S. M. P., who are charged before H. M. Supreme Court with the murder of Mau Teh-piau, a Chinese beggar, by throwing him into Hongkew Creek in the early morning of December 1, thereby causing his death from pneumonia. In spite of the unusual speed with which most of these witnesses were disposed of, the hearing lasted until 7 p.m. and will be continued this morning with the appearance of still more witnesses. Court will probably be adjourned this noon until Monday morning, so that it is not likely that the case will be finished until well into next week.

The hearing yesterday was featured chiefly by the testimony of Inspector George Joseph Bennett, in charge of Kashing Road Police Station, who was on the stand most of the afternoon, and by the reading out of two statements made by the accused and handed to the Inspector shortly after December 1, in which they state their own version of the affair.

Comedy Furnished

As usual, comedy was furnished for the crowd of interested spectators by the bickering between attorneys for the defence and the prosecution. These interludes provided some relief for the jury of 12 British residents who have been living at the Astor House since the start of the trial on Tuesday, as well as for Judge A. G. Mossop. The two accused, seated in the dock, however, maintain for the most part a silent seriousness.

The statements made by Peters and Judd, written out and given to their superior at Kashing Road Station on December 3, were read out in court by the Crown Advocate, Mr. Victor Priestwood, the judge cautioning the jury that the statement made by Peters was not evidence against Judd, and similarly that Judd's statement was not evidence against Peters. At the end of both statements was written: "Before handing this statement to Inspector Bennett, I was cautioned by him re the possibility of a serious charge being preferred against me and that this statement may be used in evidence."

Peters' Statement

The following is the statement by F. S. Peters:

"I beg to report that due to the outlook of the case in which I am involved, which now appears to be more serious than which I had at first thought, I wish to retract my former statement, which was not correct in detail, and now wish to make the following statement.

"At about 2.15 p.m. 1-12-35 I received a street telephone message from a C.P.C. to the effect that a sick beggar was lying on Point Road, near Sinkeipang Road. Having received exaggerated reports previously re beggars being sick, I decided to send a foreigner to investigate first to find out if the ambulance was required.

"P. S. Judd came to the station at 2.30 p.m. reporting for coffee, and I detailed him for this duty, as 3 a.m.-3.20 a.m. was his correct coffee time. Before he left, F. S. Makovetsky reported for coffee (2.30—2.50 a.m.)

"P. S. Judd being new to the district, I decided to accompany him, and left F. S. Makovetsky in charge of the office.

"On arrival at the scene of the report, I decided to remove the beggar in the station car to St. Luke's Hospital. When proceeding over East Hanbury Road Bridge, the beggar appeared to have recovered, so I decided to dispose of him on the nearest beggar boat on the Hongkew Creek, and turned along Fearon Road, to do so.

"With the aid of P. S. Judd, I lowered him on to a beggar boat moored alongside the creek, and then returned to the station.

"I am, Sir,
"Your obedient Servant
"(Sgd.) F. S. 229 PETERS."

Judd's Statement

The following is the statement by W. A. Judd:

"I beg to report that, owing to the seriousness of the case a more detailed report is called for, I wish to retract my previous statement and substitute the following.

"At about 2.30 a.m. on the 1st inst. I reported for coffee, on arrival at the station F. S. Peters informed me that my correct time for coffee was from 3 a.m. to 3.20 a.m. As I was on the point of going, F. S. Peters called me back and detailed me to investigate the report of a sick beggar lying on Point and Sinkeipang Roads.

"While waiting for the station car, F. S. Makovetsky also reported for coffee.

"When about to leave, F. S. Peters came out and asked me if I knew the place. I replied I did not, he then said he would accompany me. We then proceeded to the place reported. On arrival, we found a male Chinese lying on the ground. F. S. Peters remarked that he appeared to be very sick, so decided to take him to St. Luke's Hospital in the station car. Whilst proceeding along East Hanbury Road, the beggar appeared to have recovered, so we decided to put him in Chinese territory, a beggar boat on the creek being the nearest. By this time we were passing over Hanbury Road bridge. Observing a beggar boat moored on the Hongkew side of the creek, we turned down Fearon Road, stopping opposite the beggar boat, and lowered him on to the deck, after which we returned to the station.

"I am Sir,
"Your obedient Servant.
"(Sgd.) W. A. JUDD."

Bennett On Stand

Inspector Bennett took the stand about 3 p.m. yesterday. He testified that he had received a report from a Chinese detective-sergeant, Tsan Ling-vei, on December 1, and he had then made inquiries. He had looked in the station 'phone message book, and on page 98 he had found an entry, in Peters' handwriting, which read: "On arrival, the beggar had left.—A.P." He then investigated the station occurrence book, and found in Judd's handwriting: "30-11-35. P. S. Judd on duty. 10.45 p.m., paraded with duties. 11 p.m.-3 a.m., in charge of dog van; captured one wonk dog. 7 a.m., off duty."

"I called C.P.C. 3067," the inspector went on, "the station chauffeur, after looking at these books, and I obtained a statement. I also got statements from Sergeant Makovetsky and the clerk, Yuan Wong-shing, on December 2. I then phoned Captain Kennedy and he came to the station on the evening of December 2. He questioned the driver and told me to call Peters and Judd into the station for questioning individually. Judd came in first. Captain Kennedy, Judd and I were there.

Mr. Priestwood—What threat or promise did Captain Kennedy hold over his head?—None. Captain Kennedy said, "Sergeant Judd, I have a serious allegation to make against you." The Captain read the chauffeur's statement to Judd and asked him if he had anything to say. Judd replied: "It is wrong. I want time to think it over."

Both Cautioned

The Inspector went on to say that next Peters was called in. Both men had been cautioned by the Captain to consider what they were saying. The statement was again read, and Peters then made a statement to the Captain and the Inspector and signed it. (This statement was later retracted and the one quoted in full above was made.)

That evening Judd gave the Inspector his signed statement, which was also later retracted for the one quoted above.

Mr. Priestwood—Could Peters and Judd have got together during that time alone?—I didn't see them. They could have.

Inspector Bennett continued that on the evening of December 2, Captain Kennedy sent a request to the Customs River Police and at 6 a.m. on December 3, he (Bennett) went to Hongkew Creek with the driver, C.P.C. 3067. There they met a Chinese police officer, No. 75, of the River Police. Dragging operations were being conducted in the creek between Yuhang Road and Haining Road bridges. The inspector stayed 10 minutes and then left, Probationary Sergeant No. 9 of Kashing Road Station staying behind.

（批：File）
（印：FEB. 1936）
