《字林西报》，1936年2月8日，星期六

高等法院审理乞丐案
控方证人不断增加

本内特巡官与塔克医生等重要证人出庭作证，庭审历时漫长；案件无法于今日中午前结案

插科打诨、争吵不休带来喜剧色彩；宣读供词

昨日，在工部局警务处（S.M.P.）警长E. W. 彼得斯（E. W. Peters）和试用警长W. A. 贾德（W. A. Judd）谋杀中国乞丐茅德彪（Mau Teh-piau，音译）一案的续审中，大批控方证人接连出庭作证。被告被指控于12月1日凌晨将受害者抛入虹口港，导致其因肺炎死亡。尽管大多数证人的问询过程异常迅速，听证会仍持续至晚上7点，并将在今日上午继续传唤更多证人。法庭可能在今天中午休庭至下周一上午，因此案件不太可能在下周初之前审结。

昨日的听证会主要以嘉善路警察局负责人乔治·约瑟夫·本内特（George Joseph Bennett）巡官的证词为特色，他下午大部分时间都在证人席上；此外还宣读了两名被告在12月1日后不久交给该巡官的两份供词，其中陈述了他们自己对事件的版本。

喜剧插曲

如同往常一样，辩方律师与控方律师之间的争吵为感兴趣的旁观者提供了喜剧色彩。这些插曲为自周二审判开始以来一直住在礼查饭店（Astor House）的12名英国居民组成的陪审团，以及莫索普（A. G. Mossop）法官提供了一些调剂。然而，坐在被告席上的两名被告大多保持着沉默和严肃。

彼得斯和贾德于12月3日书写并交给他们在嘉善路警局上司的供词，由皇家检察官维克多·普里斯特伍德（Victor Priestwood）先生在法庭上宣读。法官提醒陪审团，彼得斯的供词不能作为针对贾德的证据，同样，贾德的供词也不能作为针对彼得斯的证据。两份供词的末尾均写道：“在将此供词交给本内特巡官之前，他曾警告我可能会被提出严重指控，且此供词可能被用作证据。”

彼得斯的供词

以下是F. S. 彼得斯的供词：

“谨报告，鉴于我所涉案件的前景现在看起来比我起初认为的更为严重，我希望撤回我之前那份细节不实的供词，现愿作出如下陈述。

“1935年12月1日下午2点15分左右，我收到一名华捕（C.P.C.）打来的街道电话消息，称有一名生病的乞丐躺在百老汇路（Point Road，今大名路）靠近新闸路（Sinkeipang Road）的地方。由于此前收到过关于乞丐生病的夸大报告，我决定先派一名外籍人员去调查，以确定是否需要救护车。

“试用警长贾德于下午2点30分到局里报到喝咖啡，我指派他去执行这项任务，因为他正确的喝咖啡时间是凌晨3点至3点20分。在他离开之前，一级警员马科维茨基（F. S. Makovetsky）来报到喝咖啡（凌晨2点30分—2点50分）。

“由于试用警长贾德对该地区不熟悉，我决定陪同他前往，并留一级警员马科维茨基负责办公室。

“到达报告地点后，我决定用警局的汽车将乞丐送往圣路加医院（St. Luke's Hospital）。当经过东汉伯里路（East Hanbury Road，今汉阳路）桥时，乞丐似乎已经恢复，所以我决定将他安置在虹口港最近的一艘丐船上，于是沿费伦路（Fearon Road，今汾阳路或附近道路，注：此处原文为Fearon Rd，当时地图对应位置需考证，暂按音译或保留原意理解，通常指靠近河边的路）驶去，以便这样做。

“在试用警长贾德的协助下，我将他放到停靠在河浜边的一艘丐船上，然后返回警局。

“先生，
“您顺从的仆人
“（签名）F. S. 229 彼得斯。”

贾德的供词

以下是W. A. 贾德的供词：

“谨报告，由于案情严重，需要一份更详细的报告，我希望撤回我之前的陈述，并替换为以下内容。

“本月1日凌晨2点30分左右，我到局里报到喝咖啡。到达警局时，一级警员彼得斯告诉我，我正确的喝咖啡时间是凌晨3点至3点20分。正当我准备离开时，一级警员彼得斯叫我回去，并指派我去调查关于一名生病的乞丐躺在百老汇路和新闸路的报告。

“在等待警车时，一级警员马科维茨基也来报到喝咖啡。

“正当我们要离开时，一级警员彼得斯走出来，问我是否知道那个地方。我回答说不知道，他便说他会陪我一起去。随后我们前往报告地点。到达后，我们发现一名中国男子躺在地上。一级警员彼得斯说他看起来病得很重，所以决定用警车送他去圣路加医院。当沿着汉伯里路行驶时，乞丐似乎已经恢复，所以我们决定把他放到中国地界，最近的就是一艘河浜上的丐船。这时我们正经过汉伯里路桥。观察到一艘丐船停泊在河浜的虹口一侧，我们转入费伦路，停在丐船对面，将他放到甲板上，之后我们返回了警局。

“先生，
“您顺从的仆人。
“（签名）W. A. 贾德。”

本内特出庭作证

本内特巡官于昨天下午3点左右出庭作证。他作证说，他在12月1日收到了一名华籍侦探警长詹灵伟（Tsan Ling-vei，音译）的报告，随后进行了查询。他查看了警局的电话记录簿，在第98页发现了一条彼得斯手写的记录，内容是：“到达时，乞丐已离开。——A.P.” 接着他调查了警局的事件记录簿，发现了贾德手写的记录：“1935年11月30日。试用警长贾德值班。晚上10点45分，列队执行任务。晚上11点至凌晨3点，负责狗车；捕获一只流浪狗。早上7点，下班。”

“查看这些记录簿后，”巡官继续说道，“我叫来了华捕3067号，即警局司机，并取得了一份供词。我还在12月2日从警长马科维茨基和职员袁旺兴（Yuan Wong-shing，音译）那里取得了供词。随后我打电话给肯尼迪（Kennedy）队长，他于12月2日晚上来到警局。他讯问了司机，并让我把彼得斯和贾德叫到警局分别进行讯问。贾德先进来。当时在场的是肯尼迪队长、贾德和我。

普里斯特伍德先生问：——肯尼迪队长对他们施加了什么威胁或承诺？——没有。肯尼迪队长说：“贾德警长，我有一项严重的指控要针对你。” 队长向贾德宣读了司机的供词，并问他有什么要说的。贾德回答说：“这是错误的。我需要时间考虑一下。”

两人均受警告

巡官接着说，随后彼得斯也被叫进来。队长曾警告两人要考虑清楚自己所说的话。再次宣读了供词，随后彼得斯向队长和巡官作了陈述并签了字。（这份供词后来被撤回，取而代之的是上面完整引用的那份。）

当晚，贾德向巡官提交了他签名的供词，该供词后来也被上面引用的那份所取代。

普里斯特伍德先生问：——在那段单独相处的时间里，彼得斯和贾德有可能串通吗？——我没看见他们。但他们有可能。

本内特巡官继续说，12月2日晚上，肯尼迪队长向海关水上警察发出请求。12月3日早上6点，他（本内特）与司机华捕3067号一同前往虹口港。在那里，他们遇到了一名水上警察局的华籍警官，编号75号。当时正在余杭路和海宁路桥之间的河段进行打捞作业。巡官停留了10分钟后离开，嘉善路警局的9号试用警长留了下来。

（批：归档）
（印：1936年2月）

page_data.en:
No Beggar-Boats
Mr. Priestwood Did you see any beggar-boats there? — No.
Did you ever see any? — Not what I would term beggar boats. There are cargo junks there.
Inspector Bennett went on to say that he returned to the station, received a report there and returned to the creek, where he saw the hawker, Sung Ching-sung, at 6 a.m. At 11 a.m. he went to St. Luke's Hospital with two C.P.C.s and a Chinese detective with the purpose of possibly identifying a man Sung had told him about. He said C.P.C. 1728 could not identify the man he had previously seen, though in a small room off Ward B he saw a man "similar to" the one C.P.C 1993 definitely identified the man in the small room.
The Crown Advocate then proceeded with questioning regarding the hours of duty at the Kashing Road Station. In answer to these questions, Inspector Bennett said that Peters was in charge of the charge room from midnight to 8 a.m. on December 1; that Judd was on patrol duty, his hours supposed to be from 10.45 p.m. to 7 a.m. (he had been at the station five or six days only); Judd had a break for coffee from 3 a.m. to 3.20 a.m. The Inspector said that Peters was to take over the office from Sergeant Johnson at midnight, and that Sergeant Makovetsky was on patrol duty from 11 p.m. to 7 a.m. Actually he was supposed to be on from 11 p.m. to 2.30 a.m. and from 3 a.m. to 5 a.m. on search party duty.
The Inspector explained that police were required to sign in the occurrence book when they went on and off duty. This book was produced in court yesterday and the Inspector said there was entry in it which he said was in Peters' handwriting made Sunday, December 1, starting at 12 a.m. The entry finished with the hour noted —8 a.m.—and the words "off duty."

McDonald Objects
This line of questioning, however, was terminated by vigorous objections from Mr. Ranald McDonald, counsel for Peters.
The Inspector continued that at noon on December 3, Peters and Judd came to his office and each gave him a written statement. (These statements are reproduced in full above.)
After the statements were read in court, Mr. McDonald asked Inspector Bennett if he had ever seen a beggar boat, to which the Inspector declared that there was no such thing, and that some cargo boats might be used by beggars but that a patrol boat from the Hongkew Police Station was used on Hongkew Creek to keep such boats from coming down into the Settlement from Chinese territory.
Mr. McDonald—This patrol boat is patrolling both night and day?
—No, only in the daytime.
This concluded Inspector Bennett's testimony.

15 Witnesses Called
Some 15 witnesses in all were called during yesterday's hearing, most of them in the morning. The first witness was C.P.C. 1665 of Hongkew Station, who said he had received a telephone message at 3.10 a.m. December 1 and reported to the sub-inspector in charge.
The second witness was the police interpreter at Hongkew Station, Chu Ming-kung, who said that he heard the C.P.C. make the report on a request for an ambulance and had registered this in the book and then sent out a Chinese detective constable.

The third witness was John Vincent Hourihan, who was on duty that morning in charge of Ambulance 82, of the Shanghai Fire Brigade, and received the call at 3.12 a.m. He said that he went to Fearon and Haining Roads, and was directed to a place about half-way between Haining and Yuhang Road bridges, where he found a Chinese man lying on the road unconscious. The man's clothes were wet and he had them removed, the man was wrapped in a blanket, put on a stretcher, loaded into the ambulance, and driven to St. Luke's Hospital. The clothing was given to the authorities there and the man was taken to the first aid room, and a certificate on his condition was signed by a doctor and taken back to the station. Artificial respiration was given, he said, as if the patient were a drowning man. The man was groaning and shivering.

"A Bare Man"
The fourth witness was Dr. Lum Ding-wong, an interne at St. Luke's in the emergency ward. He saw the man unconscious, he said, and with a temperature below 95 degrees. There was no water in the man's lungs. The witness caused some merriment in court when he described the beggar as "a bare man" (through the interpreter) in answer to a question as to whether the man was "rich or poor."
Hu Chun-sung, a male nurse at the hospital, appeared next to testify that the man arrived at 3.30 a.m. He described arrangements made to keep the patient warm, and said that the man looked "very poor."
Another nurse, Zung Tsu-lin, appeared to testify that he saw an old, weak Chinese in bed 7, Ward B, at 7 a.m. on December 1. He said the man was later transferred to bed 20 in a small room because he was groaning and disturbing other patients in the ward. On December 1, the man recovered his senses but not on December 2. The man's hair and beard were cut on December 2.
A witness, Tsa Kweh-soong, was then called but was not examined and was dismissed.

Tucker Testifies
Dr. Augustine Washington Tucker, senior medical officer of St. Luke's, then took the stand. He said that he saw Mau Teh-piau in the hospital on December 3 and examined him and found him in very serious condition, likely to die. "He was suffering from double pneumonia."
Mr. John McNeill (aiding in the prosecution)—Were you asked to make your examination from any particular point of view?—Yes. I made the examination with the view to finding out whether a deposition could be taken then or delayed.
Dr. Tucker added that he thought a statement should be taken soon, as he could not predict how long the man might live. He declared that, with the help of Dr. U. K. Koo, he questioned the man on the morning of December 3 and received coherent replies for the most part, though questions had to be repeated several times.
Mr. H. A. Reeks (counsel for Judd)—Can a doctor say when one is about to die of pneumonia?—I do not think that anyone can say that unless the patient is just at the very end.
Mr. Reeks—Is it correct that Mau Teh-piau, throughout his stay in hospital was delirious?—You might call him semi-delirious, but I wouldn't call him completely delirious.
Judge Mossop—Was there any conversation with the patient regarding his health?—He said that he had not eaten for five days before.
Judge Mossop—Any talk about the future?—No.

Deposition Barred
Judge Mossop (To Mr. Priestwood)—I've made my decision in this matter. It doesn't matter at all whether Dr. Tucker thought this man was dangerously ill or not. The point is whether or not he thought himself on the point of death.
The Judge barred the dying deposition of the patient from use as evidence. "I'm not satisfied that the mental condition of the patient was such that he had a settled, hopeless expectation of death, not qualified by hopes of recovery."
The deposition had been taken down by Mr. Anthony Ricketts, through an interpreter, at the hospital and was produced in Police Court at the preliminary trial. It alleged that Mau was thrown into the creek by two foreigners whom he could not then recognize, and that he had been in a car with them. This barring of the deposition eliminated two witnesses—Ricketts, chief clerk of the Police Court, and the Chinese interpreter.
Dr. Tucker was followed on the stand by an interne at St. Luke's, Ting Tsai-tung, who had examined Mau at 7 a.m. on December 1. At this point, there arose a legal argument over the patient's name and how it had been got, and it was held that the name should not be admitted as evidence. The judge declared that it didn't really matter anyway.
Next witness was a resident physician at St. Luke's, Dr. Kwong Ming-sing, who said he first saw Mau on the morning of December 2. He said that the patient died on December 6, and that he had signed the death certificate.
The last witness of the morning session was Detective Sub-Inspector John McFee, of Kashing Road Station. He testified that he had arrested the accused on December 4, and that he also had taken Sung, the hawker, to the hospital, where Sung had identified the man in the small room as the man he (Sung), had pulled out of the creek. When Peters and Judd were arrested, McFee stated, they each declared: "I have nothing to say."

Session Ended
This ended the morning session. The afternoon session was opened with Dr. Seth Kenneth Squires on the stand. He attended the post mortem on the patient at the Fearon Road Mortuary and described the body as that of a man of middle height, middle age, and emaciated. Mr. McFee, Mr. Rivens (mortuary attendant), Dr. Branch and three Chinese were present. It was his opinion that the man died of pneumonia. He then gave a more or less technical description of the disease, saying that there were three separate pneumonias in the lungs, one bronchial. The newest stage was about four or five days old. Lung sections had been sent in bottles to the S.M.C. laboratories.
page_data.zh:
无乞丐船
普里斯特伍德先生：你在那里看到任何乞丐船吗？——没有。
你以前见过吗？——不是我称之为乞丐船的那种。那里有货用舢板。
贝内特巡官接着说，他返回警署，在那里收到一份报告，然后又回到小河浜，在早上6点看到了小贩宋庆松（Sung Ching-sung，音译）。上午11点，他带着两名华捕和一名华探前往圣路加医院，目的是可能辨认出宋曾向他提及的一名男子。他说，华捕1728号无法辨认出他此前见过的那个人，尽管在B病房旁的一间小屋里，他看到一个“类似于”华捕1993号明确指认的那名男子的人。
王室律师随后就嘉兴路警署的值班时间问题进行提问。针对这些问题，贝内特巡官说，12月1日午夜至上午8点，彼得斯（Peters）负责看守室；贾德（Judd）在执行巡逻任务，其规定值班时间为晚上10点45分至早上7点（他在该警署仅待了五六天）；贾德在凌晨3点至3点20分之间有喝咖啡的休息时间。巡官说，彼得斯应在午夜从约翰逊（Johnson）警佐手中接管办公室，而马科维茨基（Makovetsky）警佐的巡逻值班时间为晚上11点至早上7点。实际上，他的规定值班时间是晚上11点至凌晨2点30分，以及凌晨3点至5点执行搜捕队任务。
巡官解释说，警察在上下班时必须在记事簿上签到。该记事簿已于昨天在法庭出示，巡官称其中有一条记录，他说是彼得斯在12月1日星期日写的，从午夜12点开始。该记录以注明的时间——上午8点——及“下班”字样结束。

麦克唐纳提出异议
然而，这一连串的提问因彼得斯的辩护律师拉纳德·麦克唐纳（Ranald McDonald）先生的强烈反对而终止。
巡官继续说道，12月3日中午，彼得斯和贾德来到他的办公室，各自向他提交了一份书面陈述。（这些陈述全文见上文。）
陈述在法庭宣读后，麦克唐纳先生问贝内特巡官是否见过乞丐船，巡官宣称并没有这种东西，虽然有些货船可能被乞丐使用，但虹口警署的一艘巡逻艇在虹口港巡逻，以防止此类船只从中国地界进入租界。
麦克唐纳先生：这艘巡逻艇是日夜巡逻吗？
——不，只在白天。
至此，贝内特巡官的证词结束。

传唤15名证人
在昨天的听证会上，总共传唤了约15名证人，大多数是在上午。第一位证人是虹口警署的华捕1665号，他说他在12月1日凌晨3点10分接到电话留言，并向负责的副巡官报告。
第二位证人是虹口警署的警务翻译朱明公（Chu Ming-kung，音译），他说他听到华捕报告请求救护车，并将此登记在册，随后派出一名华探。

第三位证人是约翰·文森特·胡里汉（John Vincent Hourihan），他是上海救火会第82号救护车的负责人，当天上午值班，于凌晨3点12分接到呼叫。他说他前往斐伦路和海宁路，被指引到海宁路和余杭路桥之间大约一半的地方，在那里他发现一名中国男子昏迷躺在路上。该男子的衣服湿透，被人脱下，用毯子包裹，放在担架上，抬进救护车，送往圣路加医院。衣物交给了院方当局，该男子被送入急救室，医生签署了一份关于其状况的证明并送回警署。他说，对该男子实施了人工呼吸，就像对待溺水者一样。该男子当时在呻吟和颤抖。

“一个赤身裸体的人”
第四位证人是圣路加医院急诊室的实习医生林定旺（Lum Ding-wong，音译）博士。他说他看到该男子处于昏迷状态，体温低于95度。该男子的肺里没有积水。当被问及该男子是“富还是穷”时，证人通过翻译将该乞丐描述为“一个赤身裸体的人”，这在法庭上引起了一阵欢笑。
随后出庭作证的是医院男护士胡春松（Hu Chun-sung，音译），他说该男子于凌晨3点30分到达。他描述了为使病人保暖所采取的措施，并称该男子看起来“非常贫穷”。
另一名护士宗祖林（Zung Tsu-lin，音译）出庭作证说，他在12月1日早上7点在B病房7号床看到一位年老体弱的中国人。他说，由于该男子呻吟并打扰病房里的其他病人，后来被转移到一间小屋的20号床。12月1日，该男子恢复了知觉，但12月2日没有。该男子的头发和胡须是在12月2日剪掉的。
随后传唤了一名证人查贵松（Tsa Kweh-soong，音译），但未对其进行讯问即予遣散。

塔克作证
圣路加医院的高级医务官奥古斯丁·华盛顿·塔克（Augustine Washington Tucker）博士随后出庭。他说他在12月3日在医院见到了毛德标（Mau Teh-piau，音译），对他进行了检查，发现他病情非常严重，可能会死亡。“他患有双侧肺炎。”
约翰·麦克尼尔先生（协助控方）：有人要求你从特定角度进行检查吗？——是的。我进行检查的目的是为了确定当时是否可以录取供词，还是需要推迟。
塔克博士补充说，他认为应尽快录取供词，因为他无法预测该男子还能活多久。他声明，在顾玉坤（U. K. Koo，音译）医生的帮助下，他在12月3日上午讯问了该男子，大部分问题得到了连贯的回答，尽管一些问题需要重复几次。
H. A. 里克斯先生（贾德的辩护律师）：医生能说出一个人何时将死于肺炎吗？——我认为除非病人已处于最后时刻，否则没人能说得准。
里克斯先生：毛德标在整个住院期间都处于谵妄状态，这说法正确吗？——你可以说他处于半谵妄状态，但我不会说他完全谵妄。
莫索普法官：有没有与病人谈论过他的健康状况？——他说他在此之前已有五天未进食。
莫索普法官：有没有谈论未来？——没有。

供词被排除
莫索普法官（对普里斯特伍德先生说）：我已就此事项作出决定。塔克医生认为此人病危与否根本不重要。关键在于他是否认为自己濒临死亡。
法官禁止将该病人的临终供词作为证据使用。“我不满意患者的精神状态表明他对死亡有着既定且无望的预期，且这种预期并未因康复的希望而减弱。”
该供词由安东尼·里基茨（Anthony Ricketts）先生通过翻译在医院记录，并在预审时的警察法庭出示。供词指控毛被两名当时无法辨认的外国人扔进小河浜，且他曾与他们同乘一辆汽车。排除该供词导致两名证人——警察法庭首席书记员里基茨和华语翻译——无需出庭。
继塔克博士之后出庭的是圣路加医院的实习医生丁载东（Ting Tsai-tung，音译），他曾在12月1日早上7点检查过毛。此时，围绕患者姓名及其获取方式出现了法律争论，裁定该姓名不得作为证据采纳。法官宣布无论如何这并不真正重要。
下一位证人是圣路加医院的驻院医生邝明兴（Kwong Ming-sing，音译）博士，他说他在12月2日上午首次见到毛。他说病人于12月6日死亡，他签署了死亡证明。
上午庭审的最后一名证人是嘉兴路警署的侦探副巡官约翰·麦克菲（John McFee）。他作证说，他于12月4日逮捕了被告，并且还将小贩宋某带到医院，宋某指认小屋里的那名男子就是他从河里拉出来的人。麦克菲陈述，彼得斯和贾德被捕时，各自声明：“我无话可说。”

庭审结束
上午庭审至此结束。下午庭审开始时，塞思·肯尼思·斯奎尔斯（Seth Kenneth Squires）博士出庭。他在斐伦路停尸房参加了患者的尸检，描述尸体为中等身高、中年、消瘦的男子。麦克菲先生、里文斯先生（停尸房 attendant）、布兰奇博士和三名中国人在场。他认为该男子死于肺炎。随后他对这种疾病进行了或多或少技术性的描述，称肺部有三处独立的肺炎病灶，其中一处为支气管性。最新的病灶阶段约为四五天。肺切片已装入瓶中送往工部局实验室。

Mr. Priestwood—If you were
told that a man had been tossed
into water on December 1 and
later died, what would you say?
—That the man's death was pro-
bably aided by pneumonia.
Mr. Priestwood—What would
happen to a sick man if he were
thrown into cold water?—It would
make him liable to pneumonia.
Mr. McDonald—If a man were
lying stiff and foaming at the
mouth, would you say he had acute
pneumonia?—Not unless I examin-
ed him.

Sink Or Float?
Mr. Reeks—If an unconscious
person were tossed into water,
would he sink or float?—It
depends on the water, the kind of
person, and the amount of cloth-
ing. If he were a heavily dress-
ed, thin man, he might sink.
Dr. Squires added that there
were slight abrasions on the
man's body, but that these would
not have had any part in his death.
Dir. James H. Blakelock, P.H.D.
pathologist, testified that he had
received sections of lungs on
December 6, and corroborated
Dr. Squire's evidence.
He was then followed by In-
spector Bennett.
At the close of the day when
Inspector Bennett was finished,
two last witnesses were examined
briefly — Probationary-Sergeant
John Deaville, of Kashing Road
Station, who said that on Decem-
ber 2 he saw dredging work at
Hongkew Creek and saw river
police there, and that dredging was
later stopped; and the St. Luke's
nurse Hu, who had testified be-
fore, who identified a bundle of
clothing as that brought in with
the patient. The clothing con-
sisted of very ragged blue and
black co on trousers, jacket and
gown, a ragged sweater, and a
pair of worn Chinese slippers.

"Like Mr. Punch?"
The comedy relief of the hear-
ing was furnished by various folks
present.
When Dr. Squires was describ-
ing the appearance of the man,
he said that the man had very
wide cheek-bones, sunken eyes and
a prominent chin. Judge Mossop
asked: "Do you mean that it
came forward—like Mr. Punch?"
"Yes. And his leg bones below
the knees were bowed forward."
"You mean," said the judge,
"that he was bandy-legged-for-
ward?"
Dr. Squires spoke of "red and
grey hepatisation" several times
in describing types of pneumonia.
Mr. McDonald—How do you
spell 'hepatisation'?
Judge Missop—Yes. Please spell
it—to save me asking you quietly
about that later on. (After the
word was spelled, the judge said
"Thank you!" emphatically, and
a titter ran round the room.)
When Dr. Blakelock was being
examined regarding microscopic
slides, he was asked by Mr
Priestwood if he could tell from
the slides what the man died of.
He said no.
"Why, he might have died of
a bullet in the head!" the Judge
interposed.
"I said it only in fairness to the
accused," Mr. Priestwood murmur-
ed. Mr. McDonald jumped up and
declared: "We want no fairness
from you, Mr. Priestwood!" To
which Mr. Priestwood replied:
"You'll get it anyway, Mr.
McDonald."
At another time, when Mr.
Priestwood had just opened his
mouth to put a question to In-
spector Bennett, Mr. McDonald
rose, and when asked by the Judge
what he wanted, he said: "Noth-
ing. I was just waiting for an
improper question!"

普里斯特伍德先生：如果告诉你有人在12月1日被抛入水中，后来死亡，你会怎么说？
——该男子的死亡可能由肺炎促成。
普里斯特伍德先生：如果一个病人被扔进冷水中会发生什么？——这会使他易患肺炎。
麦克唐纳先生：如果一个人躺着僵硬且口吐白沫，你会说他患有急性肺炎吗？——除非我检查过他，否则不会。

沉还是浮？
里克斯先生：如果一个昏迷的人被抛入水中，他会沉下去还是浮起来？——这取决于水的情况、人的类型以及衣着多少。如果他是一个衣着厚重、瘦弱的人，可能会下沉。
斯奎尔斯博士补充说，该男子身体上有轻微擦伤，但这些与其死亡无关。
詹姆斯·H·布莱洛克（James H. Blakelock）博士，病理学博士，作证说他在12月6日收到了肺切片，并证实了斯奎尔斯博士的证据。
随后由贝内特巡官出庭。
在当天结束时，贝内特巡官作证完毕后，简要讯问了最后两名证人——嘉兴路警署的见习警佐约翰·迪维尔（John Deaville），他说他在12月2日看到虹口港有疏浚作业，并看到水上警察在场，后来疏浚工作停止；以及此前曾作证的圣路加医院护士胡某，他辨认出一包衣物是随病人一起送来的。衣物包括非常破旧的蓝色和黑色棉裤、夹克和长袍，一件破旧的毛衣，以及一双磨损的中式拖鞋。

“像潘奇先生？”
听证会的喜剧插曲由在场的各种人士提供。
当斯奎尔斯博士描述该男子的外貌时，他说该男子颧骨很宽，眼窝凹陷，下巴突出。莫索普法官问：“你的意思是它向前突出——像潘奇先生（Mr. Punch，木偶剧角色）那样？”
“是的。而且他膝盖以下的小腿骨向前弯曲。”
“你的意思是，”法官说，“他是向前罗圈腿？”
斯奎尔斯博士在描述肺炎类型时多次提到“红色和灰色肝变”。
麦克唐纳先生：“肝变（hepatisation）怎么拼写？”
莫索普法官：是的。请拼写出来——免得我稍后悄悄问你。（单词拼写完后，法官 emphatically 地说“谢谢！”，房间里响起一阵窃笑声。）
当布莱洛克博士就显微镜切片接受讯问时，普里斯特伍德先生问他是否能从切片中看出死因。他说不能。
“哎呀，他可能是头部中弹而死！”法官插话道。
“我这么说只是为了对被告公平，”普里斯特伍德先生低声说道。麦克唐纳先生跳起来宣称：“我们不需要你的公平，普里斯特伍德先生！”对此，普里斯特伍德先生回答：“不管怎样你都会得到的，麦克唐纳先生。”
另有一次，当普里斯特伍德先生刚张开嘴要向贝内特巡官提问时，麦克唐纳先生站起身，当法官问他想要什么时，他说：“没什么。我只是在等待一个不当的问题！”

THE SHANGHAI TIMES, FRIDAY, FEBRUARY 7, 1936
Hawker Holds His Own
In Examination During
Municipal Police Trial
Witness, Counsels, Prosecutor Battle Case Out
During Prolonged Session; Station Driver
Winds Up Testimony Regarding Beggar
COURTROOM PACKED WITH SPECTATORS;
THREE OTHERS ARE CALLED
A Chinese vegetable hawker, H. M. Crown Advocate,
and attorneys for the defence combined in H.B.M. Supreme
Court yesterday to inject considerable action and colour into
the continued session of the trial of Sergeant E. W. Peters
and Probationary Sergeant W. A. Judd, S.M.P., on a charge
of murdering a Chinese beggar, Mau Teh-piau, on December
1. The hawker spoke his mind in no uncertain manner
through a weary interpreter, and the prosecution and de-
fence counsels maintained a running fire of bitter comment
and bickering throughout the day, to the edification of a
closely packed courtroom of spectators.
The day's proceedings were
marked by the conclusion of the
examination of the prosecution's
star witness, Doo Eung-foo, C.P.C.
No. 3067, chauffeur at the Kashing
Road Police Station, and the
lengthy examination of Sung
Ching-sun, the hawker who is said
to have rescued the beggar from
the Hongkew Creek. The hawker
was succeeded on the stand by
three other witnesses who gave
brief testimony before the court
was adjourned late yesterday
afternoon. The case will be resum-
ed this morning at 9.45.
Judge A. G. Mossop was able to
maintain the peace in the court
yesterday only by frequently tak-
ing over direct examination of
witnesses himself. The room was
jammed with spectators, many of
whom stood up most of the day.
The jury of 12 British residents
took a more active part in the
proceedings yesterday, several of
the members personally putting
questions that had not been satis-
fied by the questioning of the
Crown Advocate, Mr. Victor
Priestwood, assisted by Mr. John
McNeill, and Mr. Ranald Mc-
Donald for Peters and Mr. H. A.
Reeks for Judd.
Hawker Holds Up
The hawker managed to hold up
his own end of the proceedings
during the afternoon when under
a gruelling cross-examination the
defence counsels attempted to
prove that witness was not so
much a vegetable hawker as he was
"well-known as a loafer and a
pimp," and an associate of pro-
stitutes in a gaming house, to
which allegations the witness an-
swered with considerable heat and
vehemence, though he admitted
living in the same room with a
woman and of having served a
gaol term for opium smoking.
The car-driver, Doo, was in the
witness box most of the morning,
having occupied the box most of
the preceding day. The contest be-
tween counsels and prosecution
started early over the written
translation and original written
Chinese of a statement regarding
the affair signed by Doo in Decem-
ber, Mr. Reeks wanting the
original statement read out and
Mr. McDonald disassociating him-
self from Mr. Reeks in this mat-
ter. The interpreter hesitated over
the wording of the document, stat-
ing that it was written in the
"grass" characters, at which Mr.
Reeks offered to read the Chinese
himself. During the day both Mr.
Reeks and Mr. Priestwood, who
both speak and understand Chin-
ese, objected on occasion to inter-
pretations of witnesses' state-
ments, and at one place Mr.
Priestwood wanted the interpreter
replaced by another, to which Mr.
Reeks declared: "I've never heard
better interpretation in this
court!"
"With My Own Eyes"
Doo repeated his statement: "I
heard the noise of the beggar
dropping into the water and I saw
with my own eyes that the beg-
gar was thrown into the water of
the creek." He denied that the ac-
cused talked together during the
car trip on the night in question,
and said that the sick beggar did
not speak either, except to make
a moan sound.
Witness was closely questioned
as to the exact time of leaving
and returning to Kashing Road
Station, and declared that he drove
away at 2.45 a.m. and returned
at 3.06 a.m. because he had seen
the station clock through the
charge room window when leav-
ing, and had seen it again on his
return when he turned in his key.
Mr. Reeks—Don't you say it
was 3.05 a.m. because you had
heard it was about that time when
another policeman found a beggar
being pulled out of the creek?—
What beggar? What creek? I
never heard of this.
Mr. Reeks said that witness had
told the prosecution that he got
his time by looking at his own
watch, which witness then denied.
Mr. Reeks—I put it to you that
you turned your head and hid it
in your arms so that you would
not have to reply to questions as
to whether you saw a person
standing near the car.—I don't
remember.
Mr. McDonald then raised the
question of the position of the car
in the station compound.
Mr. McDonald—When you drove
out at 2.45 did you stop just in
front of the charge room
entrance?—Yes.
Mr. McDonald—If you did, it
would mean that you would have
to back up to get out of the com-
pound. Did you?—No.
Mr. McDonald—The point is, he
didn't stop directly opposite the
charge room entrance. Nor did he
get out of the car. I put it to you
that sitting in the car you couldn't
see the clock through the charge
room side window.
Could See Clock
Witness declared that he could
see the clock from the car. Ques-
tioned as to his return, he said he
drove the car into the station
garage front first. Mr. McDonald
said that police cars were sup-
posed to be backed in, with the
hood facing out, but witness re-
plied that this was true in the
daytime but on cold nights the
hood went in first.
The Crown Advocate then ask-
ed about the dog in the car on
Fearon Road, saying: "As the dog
was jumping about in the car,
didn't that distract your attention
from the right side?" The driver
agreed.
Mr. Priestwood—Where was the
beggar at that time?—He was
just thrown in.
Other questions were asked by
the Advocate regarding the
routine checks on comings and
goings of staff at the station.
Judge Mossop wished a demons-
tration of the way in which the
beggar was placed on the running
board of the car, and this was
given by the driver.
Juryman N. L. Sparke asked
why the car was stopped in
Fearon Road. The driver replied
that this was done on the order
of officer 209. Juryman H. Strachan
then asked if the driver had heard
any other noise beside the splash,
to which witness said he had not.
Mr. Strachan asked how the
beggar was dressed but the driver
could not say.
Mr. Strachan—Can you distin-
guish between the sound of water
when a person is thrown into it,
and the sound of any other kind
of a heavy object striking the
water? The witness said he could
not reply.
Hawker Called
This concluded the driver's
testimony, and Sung Ching-sun,
the vegetable hawker, was called
to the witness stand. A middle-
aged man apparently of the lower
class, he said he lived at 493
Fearon Road and that he buys his
vegetables at the Small East Gate,
Nantao, every morning at about 3
a.m. Answering questions by the
Crown Advocate, the hawker said
that he rose at 3 a.m. because he
had a clock in his room, a big
clock like the one on the court-
room wall. It made noises on the
hours.
When he went out of his house
he saw a motor car at the side of
Hongkew Creek just opposite his
door, the car facing north. It was
a black touring car and was stand-
ing still. He saw a driver inside
who "looked like a Chinese Police
Constable." He saw two foreigners
standing near the car, wearing
uniforms that "looked like those
worn by foreign police sergeants."
They were standing near the car,
about behind it, by the bund rail-
ing, and were using torch-lights.
The hawker was given a large
map of the area and marked it
to indicate these points.
"I Feel Wonderful"
"Why," Mr. Priestwood asked
him, "did you look at those men?"
This question was put to witness
as usual through the interpreter,
and the reply given by the latter
somewhat astonished the court, for
he said loudly: "I feel wonderful!"
The sentence was later amended
to "curious."
Witness—Pang leaned over the
rail. They stood as long as
three or four minutes.
File
7 FEB. 1936

《字林西报》，1936年2月7日，星期五
小贩在庭审讯问中坚守立场
证人、律师与检察官在漫长的庭审过程中激烈交锋；巡捕房司机就乞丐一案结束作证
法庭挤满旁听者；另有三人被传唤

昨日，一名中国菜贩、英王陛下最高法院的公诉人以及被告辩护律师共同在英国驻华最高法院（H.B.M. Supreme Court）进行的持续庭审中，为警长 E. W. Peters 和试用警长 W. A. Judd（二人均系上海公共租界工部局警务处人员）被控于12月1日谋杀中国乞丐茅德标（Mau Teh-piau，音译）一案注入了大量的戏剧性情节和色彩。这名小贩通过一位疲惫不堪的翻译毫不含糊地表达了自己的观点，而控方和辩方律师整天保持着激烈的评论和争吵，使挤满旁听者的法庭深受“教益”。

当天的诉讼程序以控方主要证人、嘉兴路巡捕房司机、中国警察编号3067的杜恩福（Doo Eung-foo，音译）接受讯问的结束，以及对据说从虹口港救出该乞丐的小贩宋庆孙（Sung Ching-sun，音译）的长时间讯问为标志。在该小贩之后，另有三名证人出庭作了简短证言，随后法庭于昨日下午晚些时候休庭。案件将于今天上午9点45分继续审理。

莫索普（A. G. Mossop）法官昨日仅通过频繁亲自直接讯问证人，才得以维持法庭秩序。法庭内挤满了旁听者，其中许多人大部分时间都站立着。由12名英国居民组成的陪审团在昨日的诉讼程序中发挥了更积极的作用，几名陪审员亲自提出了尚未通过英王陛下公诉人维克多·普里斯特伍德（Victor Priestwood）先生（由约翰·麦克尼尔 John McNeill 先生协助）、彼得斯的辩护律师拉纳德·麦克唐纳（Ranald McDonald）先生以及贾德的辩护律师 H. A. 里克斯（H. A. Reeks）先生的提问得到满意解答的问题。

小贩坚守立场

下午，在辩护律师严酷的交叉讯问下，小贩设法守住了自己的立场。辩护律师试图证明该证人与其说是个菜贩，不如说是“众所周知的懒汉和皮条客”，并且是赌场中妓女的同伙。面对这些指控，证人回答时情绪相当激动和强烈，尽管他承认与一名女子同住一室，并曾因吸食鸦片而坐过牢。

司机杜某上午大部分时间都在证人席上，前一天的大部分时间他也占据着该席位。控辩双方律师之间的争论很早就开始了，焦点在于杜某于12月签署的一份关于此事的陈述书的中文译文原件和原始中文文本。里克斯先生要求宣读原始陈述书，而麦克唐纳先生在此事上与里克斯先生划清界限。翻译员对该文件的措辞犹豫不决，称其是用“草”字（即草书）写成的，对此里克斯先生提出由他自己来朗读中文。当天，同样会说并懂中文的里克斯先生和普里斯特伍德先生偶尔都对证人陈述的翻译提出异议，普里斯特伍德先生曾一度要求更换翻译员，对此里克斯先生宣称：“我在这法庭上从未听过比这更好的翻译！”

“亲眼所见”

杜某重复了他的陈述：“我听到了乞丐落入水中的声音，我亲眼看到乞丐被扔进港渠的水中。”他否认被告在当晚乘车途中相互交谈，并称生病的乞丐也没有说话，除了发出呻吟声。

证人就离开和返回嘉兴路巡捕房的确切时间受到了严密讯问，他声称自己于凌晨2点45分离开，于凌晨3点06分返回，因为他在离开时透过值班室窗户看到了巡捕房的时钟，而在回来交钥匙时又看到了它。

里克斯先生——你不是说时间是凌晨3点05分吗？因为你听说当另一名警察发现有人从港渠中被拉出来时，大约就是那个时间？——什么乞丐？什么港渠？我从来没听说过这事。

里克斯先生说，证人曾告诉控方他是通过看自己的手表得知时间的，证人随即予以否认。

里克斯先生——我向你指出，你转过头并把它藏在手臂里，这样你就不必回答是否看到有人站在车旁的问题。——我不记得了。

随后，麦克唐纳先生提出了汽车在巡捕房大院内位置的问题。

麦克唐纳先生——你在2点45分开出去时，是否正好停在值班室入口前？——是的。

麦克唐纳先生——如果是这样，那就意味着你必须倒车才能驶出大院。你倒了吗？——没有。

麦克唐纳先生——关键在于，他没有直接停在值班室入口对面。他也没有下车。我向你指出，坐在车里，你无法透过值班室的侧窗看到时钟。

能看到时钟

证人声称他从车里能看到时钟。当被问及返回情况时，他说他是车头朝前开进巡捕房车库的。麦克唐纳先生说，警车按规定应该倒车入库，车头朝外，但证人回答说这在白天是这样，但在寒冷的夜晚，车头是先朝里的。

随后，公诉人询问了关于斐伦路（Fearon Road）上车上的狗的情况，说道：“既然狗在车里跳来跳去，难道没有分散你对右侧的注意力吗？”司机表示同意。

普里斯特伍德先生——当时乞丐在哪里？——他刚被扔进去。

公诉人就巡捕房员工出入的常规检查提出了其他问题。

莫索普法官希望演示一下乞丐被放置在汽车踏板上的方式，司机进行了演示。

陪审员 N. L. 斯帕克（N. L. Sparke）询问为何汽车在斐伦路停下。司机回答说这是遵照209号警官的命令执行的。随后，陪审员 H. 斯特拉坎（H. Strachan）询问司机除了溅水声外是否听到其他声音，证人回答说没有。

斯特拉坎先生询问乞丐的穿着，但司机说不出来。

斯特拉坎先生——你能区分一个人被扔进水里时的水声，与其他重物击打水面的声音吗？证人说他无法回答。

传唤小贩

司机的证词至此结束，菜贩宋庆孙被传唤至证人席。他是一名看似下层阶级的中年男子，他说他住在斐伦路493号，每天凌晨3点左右去南市小东门买蔬菜。在回答公诉人的提问时，小贩说他凌晨3点起床是因为房间里有一个钟，一个像法庭墙上那样的大钟。它会在整点时发出声响。

当他走出家门时，他看到虹口港边正对着他门口的一侧停着一辆汽车，车头朝北。那是一辆黑色的 touring car（游览车/敞篷车），静止不动。他看到里面有一名司机，“看起来像一名华捕”。他看到两名外国人站在车附近，穿着“看起来像外籍巡长制服”的衣服。他们站在车附近，大约在车后方，靠着外滩栏杆，并使用手电筒。

小贩拿到了一张该地区的大地图，并做了标记以指示这些地点。

“我感觉好极了”

“为什么，”普里斯特伍德先生问他，“你要看那些人？”

这个问题像往常一样通过翻译向证人提出，后者给出的回答让法庭有些惊讶，因为他大声说道：“我感觉好极了！（I feel wonderful!）”这句话后来被修正为“好奇”。

证人——庞（Pang，音译）俯身靠在栏杆上。他们站了大概三四分钟。

档案
1936年2月7日

Thus statement also caused some
confusion until Judge Mossop sug-
gested it was a Chinese colloquial
comparable to "two shakes of a
duck's tail."
Witness—Then they got into the
car and were driven off toward
the north. I saw the car number
8502. There was a light on the car
near the number plate. I walked
and looked into the creek and saw

a man in the water. He was bob-
bing up and down.
Mr. Priestwood—How long after
the foreigners left the rail was
it till you saw this man in the
water?—Very little time. I saw
bubbles.
Questioned as to distances, he
said that the man was about four
feet from the bund wall.
Witness—I shouted out "ju
ming, ju ming" (save life, save
life.) Witness went on to say that
there was a boat in the creek near
the man.
Mr. Priestwood—How far was it
from the man?—About two Chin-
ese house-fronts north.
Witness marked the map to show
this. He declared it was an empty
cargo boat.
No Beggar Boat
Mr. Priestwood—Was it a beg-
gar boat?—No, no! This concluded
the morning session at 12.30 p.m.
Court was resumed again at 2.30
p.m.
With the hawker again on the
stand, Mr. Priestwood continued
How many boats were there in the
creek?—I don't know.
How many did you see?—Only
one. It looked like a firewood boat.
Did you see any beggar boats?—
I wasn't going to take a photo-
graph so I didn't notice!
Continuing, witness said: A
boatman was sleeping in the boat.
He was aroused by my cries. I
asked him for a long bamboo pole.
He gave me one. It had a hook
on the end. I told the man in the
water to grab the end. The man
was insensible. I hooked onto his
jacket. Other people came. The
boatman got his boat near to the
man in the water. The boatman
pulled the man up with his hands.
This testimony was interspersed
with frequent questions and con-
siderable objections, chiefly from
Mr. McDonald, so that finally
Judge Mossop said: "We will get
on much quicker with this if you
will refrain from unjustified inter-
ruptions!"
Crowd Gathered
Witness said another man came
along to help, and other people
gathered to watch. They got him
out of the water and put the man
on the ground by the railing. A
Chinese police constable then ap-
proached, and witness said he was
No. 933. The constable spoke to
the hawker and then went away
toward Haining Road Bridge (pre-
sumably to telephone.) He was
away a short time and then re-
turned. They waited for the
ambulance, which came from the
direction of the bridge.
About at this point the
testimony was again interrupted
by a long discussion as to the
policeman's report book, pencil,
what he said and what the hawker
said and whether the hawker
wrote anything in the book.
The hawker then went on to say
that the ambulance stopped before
his house, and the crew got out
with a stretcher. They took off
the man's wet clothing, put him
on the stretcher, wrapped him in
a blanket, put him into the
ambulance, took his clothing along,
and drove away toward the south.
C.F.C. 933 went with the ambul-
ance.
Questioned as to the victim's
clothing, the hawker said he wore
long black trousers and a jacket,
but had not seen them clearly.

Viewed In Hospital
He saw this man again on
December 3 in a small room in
St. Luke's Hospital. He said he
was taken there by a foreigner
whom he supposed to be the "head"
of the Kashing Road Station.
Mr. Priestwood—Did you notice
any change in the man in the
hospital?—Yes. His long hair and
beard had been cut off.
Mr. Reeks then began his cross-
examination, and his first question
produced an answer that caused
considerable amusement.
"Why," Mr. Reeks asked, "as you
said before, were you 'curious'
about the foreigners when you
saw them by the railing?" "Be-
cause," the hawker replied, "I was
born in Shanghai and I have seen
and heard of many curious things
here!"
Mr. Reeks—I put it to you that
you didn't see any car there at
any time that night.—(Indignant-
ly) Why didn't I see it?
Judge Mossop—He is suggesting
that you are not telling the truth.
—That's not right.
Mr. Reeks—Why did you take
the number of the car?—Because
it was late and cold and no cars
ever stop in front of my house.
Mr. Reeks—You say you've seen
many wonderful and curious
things in Shanghai. Did you ever
take a car number before on one
of these curious occasions?—No.
But I've heard of other people
doing it.
Asked if he was not excited
about the man in the water, wit-
ness said he was "but I remem-
bered the car number."
Mr. Reeks—Was the road wet?
—No, dry.
Judge Mossop—Was it raining?
—No. (The police chauffeur had
previously testified that it was
raining quite hard.)
Mr. Reeks—I suggest that your
memory and powers of perception
are very bad.
Later witness said that the man
had been pulled out of the water
and over the bund railing. Mr.
Reeks said that in the police court
the witness had declared that the
man was pulled under the railing.
Mr. Reeks—You said it was not
a beggar boat. What is a beggar
boat like?—I don't know.
Mr. Reeks—I put it to you that
you aren't a hawker.—Then what
do I do!
Mr. Reeks—I put it to you that
you are well-known as a loafer
and a pimp!
Mr. Priestwood (rising)—Is the
defence counsel attacking the
character of the witness?
Judge Mossop — Well, rather,

That isn't exactly a term of
endearment!
Witness (referring to Mr. Reeks'
last statement).—You'll have to
prove it!
Judge Mossop—Answer the ques-
tion, yes or no.—No.
Attacking Witness
Mr. Reeks—Are you not living
with a prostitute?—That has no
connection with this case.
Mr. Reeks—Have you ever been
in gaol?—Yes, for opium smoking.
Mr. McDonald then took over the
cross-examination.
Mr. McDonald—Have you not
taken an oath here to tell the
truth?—Yes.
Mr. McDonald—Do you say that
you are not a pimp?—My profes-
sion has nothing to do with this.
Anyway, I am not a pimp.
Mr. McDonald—Is not house
number 498 on Fearon Road a
gambling house and a brothel?—
Some of the occupants are not
very respectable.
Mr. McDonald—Do you live on
the top floor?—I live downstairs.
Mr. McDonald—Do you sleep
downstairs in the front room?—I
sleep in the back room.

Mr. McDonald—Do any other
people stay in that room? Witness
denied this, saying that a large
family lived in the front room, but
finally said that a woman stayed
in the back room where he slept.
Three Others Called
This exchange practically con-
cluded the testimony given by
Sung, which was concluded at the
end of the cross-examination.
Witness left the box and was suc-
ceeded by one Say I-tse, a Chinese
pedestrian who had been passing
the spot on Fearon Road at the
time in question when the man in
the water was hauled out onto the
bunding.
Say I-tse, being called, gave
brief testimony, chiefly to the
effect that he had been passing
along Fearon Road and had been
present to see a man pulled out of
the Hongkew Creek. He had lent
some slight aid in the affair, he
said, though another man had done
most of the rescue work.
The next witness called also
gave very brief testimony. This
was a Chinese woman named
Chang Ah-sse. She lived near the
scene and at that hour of the
morning she had risen to prepare
some medicine for a sick relative.
She was attracted by a noise, look-
ed out of her house and saw
several people standing near the
bund railing. They were, she said,
lifting a man out of the creek.
She went out to have a closer look
and then returned, taking no actual
part in the affair. Some days later
she saw some men dragging the
bottom of the creek at that spot.
The last witness of the day was
Chinese Police Constable 933, who,
taking the stand, testified that he
had been on Fearon Road on patrol
that morning, and he had arrived
at the scene to find a small crowd
and a man prostrate on the ground
beside the railing. After a very
brief examination he had gone off
to the nearest police telephone box
and had telephoned for an ambul-
ance from the nearest station. The
ambulance had come and taken the
man away.
At the close of the afternoon
session, which lasted quite late,
the counsels for the defence agreed
that the Crown Advocate, Mr.
Priestwood, might ask leading
questions of witnesses in his ex-
amination henceforth. The session
was then adjourned to this morn-
ing.

因此，这一陈述也引起了一些困惑，直到莫索普（Mossop）法官指出，这是一句中国俗语，相当于“鸭子尾巴摇两下”（意指极短的时间）。

证人——随后他们上了车，向北驶去。我看到了车牌号8502。车牌附近的车上有一盏灯。我走过去向浜里张望，看见

水里有一个男人。他在水中上下起伏。

普里斯特伍德（Priestwood）先生——外国人离开栏杆后，过了多久你才看到水里的这个人？——时间很短。我看到了气泡。

当被问及距离时，他说那个人离外滩护墙大约四英尺。

证人——我大声喊叫“救命，救命”（save life, save life）。证人接着说，浜里靠近那个人的地方有一艘船。

普里斯特伍德先生——离那个人有多远？——大约在北面两个门面宽度的距离。

证人在地图上做了标记以显示此位置。他声称那是一艘空的货船。

并非乞丐船

普里斯特伍德先生——那是乞丐船吗？——不，不！上午庭审于下午12:30结束。

法庭于下午2:30重新开庭。

小贩再次出庭作证，普里斯特伍德先生继续问道：

浜里有多少艘船？——我不知道。

你看到了多少艘？——只有一艘。看起来像是一艘柴火船。

你看到任何乞丐船了吗？——我又不是要去拍照，所以我没注意！

证人继续说道：一个船夫在船上睡觉。他被我的喊叫声惊醒。我向他要一根长竹竿。他给了我一根。竹竿末端有一个钩子。我叫水里的那个人抓住末端。那个人已经失去知觉。我用钩子钩住了他的夹克。其他人走了过来。船夫将船划到靠近水中那个人的地方。船夫用手将那个人拉了上来。

这段证词期间穿插着频繁的提问和大量的反对意见，主要来自麦克唐纳（McDonald）先生，以至于最后莫索普法官说：“如果你们不进行无理的打断，我们的进展会快得多！”

人群聚集

证人说另一个人过来帮忙，其他人也聚集围观。他们把他从水里弄出来，将那人放在栏杆旁的地面上。随后一名中国巡捕走近，证人说他是933号。该巡捕与小贩交谈后，便朝海宁路桥方向走去（推测是去打电话）。他离开了一小会儿后返回。他们等待救护车，救护车从桥的方向驶来。

大约在此时，证词再次因一场漫长的讨论而中断，讨论内容涉及巡捕的报告簿、铅笔、他说了什么、小贩说了什么，以及小贩是否在报告簿上写了什么。

小贩接着说，救护车停在他家门前，医护人员带着担架下车。他们脱掉那人的湿衣服，将他放在担架上，用毯子裹好，放入救护车，带上他的衣物，然后向南驶去。华捕933号随救护车一同前往。

当被问及受害者的衣着时，小贩说他穿着黑色长裤和一件夹克，但他没有看清楚。

在医院探视

12月3日，他在圣路加医院（St. Luke's Hospital）的一个小房间里再次见到了这个人。他说是一名外国人带他去那里的，他推测此人是嘉兴路捕房的“头目”。

普里斯特伍德先生——你在医院注意到那个人有什么变化吗？——是的。他的长发和胡须都被剪掉了。

随后，里克斯（Reeks）先生开始进行交叉盘问，他的第一个问题就引出了一个引起极大哄笑的回答。

“为什么，”里克斯先生问道，“如你之前所说，当你看到栏杆旁的外国人时，你对他们感到‘好奇’？”“因为，”小贩回答道，“我出生在上海，我在这里见过并听说过许多稀奇古怪的事情！”

里克斯先生——我向你指出，那天晚上你根本没有看到那里有任何汽车。——（愤怒地）我为什么没看到？

莫索普法官——他的意思是你在说谎。——那不对。

里克斯先生——你为什么记下汽车号码？——因为当时天色已晚且天气寒冷，从来没有汽车停在我家门前。

里克斯先生——你说你在上海见过许多奇妙和稀奇的事情。在这些稀奇场合中，你以前记过汽车号码吗？——没有。但我听说过别人这样做。

当被问及对水里的那个人是否不感到激动时，证人说他是“激动的，但我记住了汽车号码”。

里克斯先生——路面是湿的吗？——不，是干的。

莫索普法官——下雨了吗？——没有。（此前警察司机已作证说雨下得很大。）

里克斯先生——我认为你的记忆力和感知力非常差。

后来证人说，那个人是从水里被拉出来并翻过外滩栏杆的。里克斯先生说，在警察法庭上，证人曾声称那个人是从栏杆下方被拉出来的。

里克斯先生——你说那不是乞丐船。乞丐船是什么样子的？——我不知道。

里克斯先生——我向你指出，你不是一个小贩。——那我做什么！

里克斯先生——我向你指出，你是个众所周知的懒汉和皮条客！

普里斯特伍德先生（起身）——辩护律师是在攻击证人的人格吗？

莫索普法官——嗯，算是吧，

那确实不是一个亲昵的称呼！

证人（提及里克斯先生的最后一句话）。——你得证明这一点！

莫索普法官——回答这个问题，是或否。——否。

攻击证人

里克斯先生——你不是和一个妓女住在一起吗？——这与本案无关。

里克斯先生——你坐过牢吗？——坐过，因为吸食鸦片。

随后麦克唐纳先生接手进行交叉盘问。

麦克唐纳先生——你在这里宣誓说过要讲真话吗？——是的。

麦克唐纳先生——你说你不是皮条客吗？——我的职业与此无关。无论如何，我不是皮条客。

麦克唐纳先生——费伦路（Fearon Road）498号不是一家赌场和妓院吗？——有些住户不太正派。

麦克唐纳先生——你住在顶层吗？——我住在楼下。

麦克唐纳先生——你睡在楼下的前屋吗？——我睡在后屋。

麦克唐纳先生——还有其他人住在那个房间吗？证人否认了这一点，称前屋住着一个大家庭，但最后他说有一个女人住在他睡觉的后屋。

另外三人被传唤

这番问答实际上结束了宋（Sung）的证词，证词在交叉盘问结束时终结。

证人离开证人席，由赛义泽（Say I-tse，音译）接替，他是一名中国行人，事发时正经过费伦路现场，当时水里的那个人正被拖到外滩护墙上。

赛义泽出庭作证，提供了简短的证词，主要内容是他当时正沿着费伦路行走，目睹了一个人从虹口浜被拉出水面。他说他在那件事中提供了一点微薄的帮助，尽管大部分救援工作是由另一个人完成的。

下一位被传唤的证人也提供了非常简短的证词。这是一位名叫张阿四（Chang Ah-sse，音译）的中国妇女。她住在现场附近，当天早晨那个时刻，她起床为生病的亲属准备药物。她被噪音吸引，从家里向外看，看到几个人站在外滩栏杆附近。她说，他们正把一个人从浜里拉上来。她走出去近距离查看，然后返回，并未实际参与此事。几天后，她看到一些人在该地点打捞浜底。

当天的最后一位证人是华捕933号，他出庭作证说，那天早上他正在费伦路巡逻，到达现场时发现有一小群人，以及一名男子俯卧在栏杆旁的地面上。经过非常简短的检查后，他前往最近的警亭，并从最近的警局打电话呼叫救护车。救护车赶到并将那人带走。

在持续至很晚的下午庭审结束时，辩护方律师同意公诉人普里斯特伍德先生此后在询问证人时可以提出诱导性问题。随后休庭，直至次日上午。

THE SHANGHAI SUNDAY TIMES. FEBRUARY 9, 1936

Prosecution's Case Against
Police Officers Closed

Defence Opens With Testimony By Sergeant Peters,
Who Repeats Lower Court Story; Admits Arriving
At Station Late Because Of Date With Girl

Public interest in the trial in
H. M. Supreme Court of Sergeant
F. W. Peters and Probationary
Sergeant W. Judd, of the Shang-
hai Municipal Police, arraigned
on charges of murder in connec-
tion with the death of Mau Tuh-
piau, a Chinese beggar, quickened
yesterday morning when the case
for the prosecution was closed by
Mr. Victor Priestwood, the Crown
Advocate, and Sergeant Peters
entered the witness-box to give
evidence in his own defence.

Sergeant Peters is represented
by Mr. Ranald G. McDonald, while
Probationary Sergeant Judd is
represented by Mr. H. A. Reeks.
According to the indictment, the
accused threw the beggar into
Hongkew Creek on the morning
of December 1, the victim dying
subsequently in St. Luke's Hos-
pital of double pneumonia.

When the Court resumed yester-
day morning, the prosecution called
Lang Soong-ching, a Chinese
Police Constable attached to the
River Police, who dragged the
creek shortly after the happening
on which the murder charge is
based, but both prosecution and
defence intimated that they had
no questions to ask him and the
witness stepped down.

Captain Kennedy Called

His place was immediately taken
in the witness-box by Captain Ed-
ward Richard Kennedy, Assistant
Commissioner of the S.M.P. This
witness testified that he had
spoken to both accused on Decem-
ber 2, informing them that the
chauffeur of the Kashing Road
Station police car had made a
statement regarding their alleged
action in throwing the beggar into
the creek the day previous.

"I told them," the witness said,
"that there might be serious
charges and cautioned them in re-
gard to the making of statements."
Nevertheless, Peters elected to
make a written statement.

Under cross-examination by Mr.
Reeks, the witness was asked
whether Judd, when the chauffeur's
statement was read to him, did not
reply: "That's a lie. I did not
throw him in the creek."

Captain Kennedy said he did not
remember Judd making any such
statement.

Mr. Reeks: Has Judd served
under you a long time?
Captain Kennedy: Yes.
Excellent Character

Mr. Reeks: Would you say of
Judd's character that it was ex-
cellent?
Captain Kennedy: Yes.
Mr. Reeks: Clean living, sport-
ing?
Captain Kennedy: Yes.
Replying to Mr. McDonald, wit-
ness said he did not know Peters
as well as he knew Judd.

This closed the case for the
prosecution and Mr. McDonald
then informed the Court that the
defence proposed to call only two
witnesses, namely, the two accus-
ed themselves.

Defence Opens

Sergeant Peters then entered
the witness box and, in reply to
questions by Mr. MacDonald, told
the Court that he was born at
Dover, county of Kent, in 1904. In
1922 he joined the Royal Tank
Corps and went to India.
Discharged from the Corps in 1929,
he returned to England.

When discharged, witness said,
he was given an exemplary char-
acter, the written record of which
he could produce if necessary. He
added that he was a first class
driver-mechanic for Rolls Royce
motor cars.

Peters then went on to relate
that he joined the S.M.P. in Lon-
don and took up duty with the
force on November 27, 1929.

Mr. McDonald asked the wit-
ness to relate what happened dur-
ing the early morning of Decem-
ber 1, when the alleged occurrence
on which the charge hinges took
place.

"I came on duty at Kashing
Road Station at 2.29 a.m.," Peters
said.

Mr. McDonald: And what time
were you supposed to have come
on?
Peters: At midnight.
Reason For Being Late

Mr. McDonald: Would you care
to say anything now as to the
reason why you were two hours
and 20 minutes late?
Peters: I had a business con-
tract to execute.

Witness then went on to repeat
the story which he told in the
lower court, declaring that he and
the other accused had taken the
sick beggar and placed him on a
beggar boat when they discovered
that he was not as sick as had
been reported. He had accom-
panied Judd on the assignment be-
cause the latter had only been at
the station five days and he (wit-
ness) wanted to satisfy himself
that the beggar was really as sick
as he was supposed to be, since
the hospitals would not admit
beggars who were not seriously ill.

The Crown Advocate then rose
to cross-examine the witness, first
asking him whether it was not
absolutely essential for the Charge
Room sergeant not to leave the
station.

Breach Of Regulations

Peters admitted that in leaving
the station he had committed a
breach of the police regulations, a
fact which he advanced as reason
for making a statement which the
defence previously admitted to be
false.

Replying to further questions,
Peters denied that he and Judd
had found the beggar "stretched
out in a very serious condition and
groaning and shivering," or that
the beggar was unconscious.

Countering this, the Crown Ad-
vocate suggested that the accus-
ed had dragged the beggar to the
police car.

Peters: We assisted him to the
car. He was very weak.

Judge Mossop: Was the beggar
able to put one foot in front of
the other?
Peters: Well, he was trying to
walk.

Carried On Running Board

Witness then denied that the
beggar was so weak as to need
conveyance in an ambulance, but
admitted that an improper use had
been made of the station car to
carry the beggar, who, according
to his testimony, was carried on
the running board. The accused
did not want to put the beggar
inside the car because beggars
were often diseased.

Questioned by the Crown Ad-
vocate as to the reason why he
came to station so late on the
morning of December 1, Peters
hesitantly admitted that the "busi-
ness contract" which detained him
was a date with "a girl friend."

The Court will sit again at 10
a.m. to-morrow and it is consider-
ed possible that the evidence and
summing-up may be concluded by
the afternoon.

（批：File 8 FEB. 1936）

《上海星期泰晤士报》。1936年2月9日

控方对警务人员的指控结案

辩方开场，由彼得斯巡长作证，
重述下级法院供词；承认因与女友约会而迟到到局

昨日晨间，随着皇家检察官维克多·普里斯特伍德先生（Mr. Victor Priestwood）结束控方陈述，以及被告彼得斯巡长（Sergeant F. W. Peters）进入证人席为自身辩护提供证词，公众对英国在华最高法院审理的上海公共租界工部局警务处彼得斯巡长和见习巡长贾德（W. Judd）谋杀案的兴趣迅速升温。该案指控二人与中国乞丐毛土标（Mau Tuh-piau，音译）之死有关。

彼得斯巡长由拉纳德·G·麦克唐纳先生（Mr. Ranald G. McDonald）代理辩护，见习巡长贾德由H·A·里克斯先生（Mr. H. A. Reeks）代理辩护。根据起诉书，被告于12月1日早晨将这名乞丐扔进虹口港（Hongkew Creek），受害者随后在圣路加医院（St. Luke's Hospital）死于双侧肺炎。

昨晨法庭复庭后，控方传唤了隶属于水上警察队的中国警员郎松庆（Lang Soong-ching，音译）。他在发生谋杀指控所依据的事件后不久曾打捞过该河道，但控辩双方均表示无意向其提问，该证人随即退庭。

肯尼迪上尉出庭作证

爱德华·理查德·肯尼迪上尉（Captain Edward Richard Kennedy），上海公共租界工部局警务处助理总监，随即接替其位置进入证人席。该证人作证称，他曾在12月2日与两名被告谈话，告知他们嘉兴路警局警车的司机已就他们前一天涉嫌将乞丐扔进河道的行为作了陈述。

“我告诉他们，”证人说，“可能会面临严重指控，并告诫他们在作出陈述时要谨慎。”尽管如此，彼得斯仍选择提交一份书面陈述。

在里克斯先生的交叉盘问下，证人被问及当向他宣读司机的陈述时，贾德是否没有回答：“那是谎言。我没有把他扔进河里。”

肯尼迪上尉表示他不记得贾德说过这样的话。

里克斯先生：贾德在您手下服役很久了吗？
肯尼迪上尉：是的。
品行优良

里克斯先生：您是否会说贾德的品行是优良的？
肯尼迪上尉：是的。
里克斯先生：生活作风正派，具有体育精神？
肯尼迪上尉：是的。
在回答麦克唐纳先生的提问时，证人表示他对彼得斯的了解不如对贾德那样深。

至此，控方陈述结束。麦克唐纳先生随后告知法庭，辩方计划仅传唤两名证人，即两名被告本人。

辩方开场

彼得斯巡长随后进入证人席，在回答麦克唐纳先生的提问时，他告诉法庭自己于1904年出生在肯特郡的多佛尔。1922年他加入皇家坦克团并前往印度。1929年从该团退役后，他返回英国。

证人称，退役时他获得了“模范品行”的评价，如有必要，他可以出示相关书面记录。他补充说，他是劳斯莱斯汽车的一级驾驶机械师。

彼得斯接着讲述了他于伦敦加入上海公共租界工部局警务处，并于1929年11月27日开始在该警队任职的经历。

麦克唐纳先生请证人叙述12月1日凌晨发生的情况，即指控所依据的所谓事件发生时的经过。

“我在凌晨2点29分到嘉兴路警局上班，”彼得斯说。

麦克唐纳先生：那你本应该几点到？
彼得斯：午夜。
迟到原因

麦克唐纳先生：您现在愿意说明一下您迟到了两小时二十分钟的原因吗？
彼得斯：我要去履行一项业务合同。

证人随后重复了他在下级法院讲述的故事，声称他和另一名被告将那名生病的乞丐带上了一艘乞丐船，因为他们发现他的病情并不像报告的那样严重。他陪同贾德执行这项任务，是因为后者刚到警局五天，而他（证人）想亲自确认这名乞丐是否真的像被认为的那样病重，因为医院不会接收病情不严重的乞丐。

皇家检察官随即起身对证人进行交叉盘问，首先问他作为值班室巡长，不离警局是否并非绝对必要。

违反规章

彼得斯承认，离开警局违反了警察规章，他将此作为此前辩方已承认为虚假的陈述的理由。

在回答进一步的问题时，彼得斯否认他和贾德发现乞丐“躺在那里，状况非常严重，呻吟且颤抖”，也否认乞丐当时处于昏迷状态。

对此，皇家检察官提出反驳，暗示被告是将乞丐拖到警车上的。

彼得斯：我们是扶他上车的。他非常虚弱。

莫索普法官：乞丐能一只脚迈在另一只脚前面走路吗？
彼得斯：嗯，他试图行走。

站在踏板上运送

证人随后否认乞丐虚弱到需要救护车运送的程度，但承认违规使用了警局车辆来运送乞丐，据其证词，乞丐是被放在车外的踏板上运送的。被告不想让乞丐坐在车内，因为乞丐往往患有传染病。

当皇家检察官询问他在12月1日早晨如此晚到达警局的原因时，彼得斯犹豫地承认，耽搁他的“业务合同”其实是与一位“女朋友”的约会。

法庭将于明日上午10点再次开庭，预计证据呈现和总结陈词可能在下午结束。

（批注：档案 1936年2月8日）

THE SHANGHAI TIMES, THURSDAY, FEBRUARY 6, 1936

Police Chauffeur Takes
Stand All Day In Trial
Of 2 Foreign Sergeants

Witness Undergoes Gruelling Examination Regard-
ing Alleged Murder Of Beggar On Fearon Road;
Driver Sticks To Lower Court Story

CASE TO BE CONTINUED THIS MORNING;
THREE WITNESSES TESTIFY IN COURT

“I have been asked so many questions to-day by so
many different people that I don’t know what to say about
anything!”

Chinese Police Constable No. 3067, Doo Sung-foo, was
reeling in the witness box in H. B. M. Supreme Court yester-
day afternoon when he said this, through the interpreter,
to Judge A. G. Mossop. After gruelling hours in the box
during both the morning and afternoon session, the police
chauffeur was taken violently ill and had to leave the Court
about 6 p.m. for a few minutes before proceedings could be
continued. The interpreter himself was so tired that he
had to be relieved by a substitute.

The chauffeur was in the box
most of yesterday’s session in the
trial of Sergeant E. W. Peters and
Probationary Sergeant W. A. Judd,
S.M.P., on a charge of murdering
a Chinese beggar, Mau Teh-piau,
on the morning of December 1.
A Shantung man speaking no
English, he quietly stood hour
after hour answering questions
put by attorneys of the prosecu-
tion and the defence and by the
judge, translated by an inter-
preter, giving evidence regarding
events on the fateful night when
the accused are alleged to have
picked up the sick Chinese beggar
and deliberately thrown him over
the bund railing into Hongkew
Creek. The chauffeur was not the
only witness to testify during the
day, but he took up most of the
time.

Court Packed

The Court was as packed on the
second day of the proceedings as
on the first in spite of the miser-
able, wet weather. The jury of
12 British residents, who had spent
the night in the Astor House
Hotel, was very attentive in spite
of the passage of hours, following
minute details in testimony care-
fully, as brought out by the Crown
Advocate, Mr. Victor Priestwood,
assisted by Mr. John McNeill, and
by the defence, Mr. Ronald Mc-
Donald and Mr. H. A. Reck.

Court opened at 9.45 a.m., the
session was adjourned at 12.30
p.m., resumed at 2.15 p.m. and
closed for the day at 6.45. The
case will be resumed this morning
at 9.45, when the chauffeur will
again go on the stand.

The first witness yesterday was
the Chinese telephone clerk of the
Kashing Road Police Station,
Yuen Wang-sheng. He testified
that at 2.45 a.m. on December 1,
he received a message over the
‘phone from C.P.C. 1728 to the
effect that “a beggar is lying in
Sinkeipang Road in a very serious
condition.” C.P.C. 1728 had testi-
fied to this the previous day, hav-
ing been on patrol that night with
C.P.C. 1193.

The report, witness declared,
was transmitted to Sergeant
Peters, in authority in the charge
room of the station. He told Ser-
geant Makovetsky, who was pre-
sent, to investigate the case, but
changed his mind because Serge-
ant Judd, who come in from patrol
made a remark, testified to be:
Sergeant Makovetsky, that Peters
had “already seen this Chinese
beggar.” Witness said that Peters
and Judd then left the charge
room, the latter taking a dog with
him, and boarded a station car
driven by C.P.C. 3067.

Drove Station Car

This chauffeur then took the
stand and stayed there the rest of
the day, being generally considered
as the prosecution’s star wit-
ness. Doo stated that he had been
a policeman in Shanghai for over
five years, most of this time at
Kashing Road Station, and was 33
years old. Previously he had been
a brass-smith. He appeared in
court in uniform.

The car he drove was a Ford
touring model carrying illuminated
licence plates, S.M.C., No. 8502,
and bearing two headlights. On
the morning in question, the two
foreign officers got into his car and
were driven from the station, turn-
ing into Urga Road and passing
Hailar Road and coming to Point
Road, on which they travelled to
Sinkeipang Road.

“When I stopped there, both for-
eigners got out. They walked to
the rear of the car. I saw them
carrying a beggar and walking
towards the car. They picked him
up in the entry to an alleyway.
One supported the beggar’s arm,
and the other held the beggar’s
other arm. The dog followed.
When they came to the car, the
beggar made a noise from his
nose, like ‘hu, hu!’ ”

Prosecutor and judge both tried
to imitate the sound with indiffer-
ent success.

Placed On Mud Guard

“I couldn’t see if the beggar was
able to walk,” witness continued.
“The two foreigners put him on
the mud guard, head in front and
feet at back.” The upper part of
the body was placed on the front
fender and the lower part on the
running board.

Peters stood on the running
board and Judd sat in the back of
the car holding the dog. The car
went to Hanbury Road, turned
right into Nanzing Road. When
the chauffeur was asked by the
Crown Advocate why he drove in
this direction, he replied that he
started towards Hongkew because
“that was the place they usually
took beggars.”

Peters told the driver to stop at
the corner of Nanzing Road and
“change the direction” of the car,
by which he meant “turn around.”
“He wanted me to drive towards
Fearon Road. They then drove to
a point between Yuhang Road
Bridge and Haining Road Bridge
on Fearon Road, where the driver
was again told to stop “about
three or four paces from the rail.”

The foreigners got out of the
car, witness said, and “took down
the beggar,” holding him by his
arms and legs. “After they got
hold of him, they walked a few
steps in the same direction the car
had been going. They threw him
down into the creek head first!”

The court asked for a demon-
stration of this.

Afternoon Session

The afternoon session was de-
voted to careful examination of all
this evidence, with considerable
cross-examination. Mr. Priestwood
questioned the driver on minute
points for some time. Mr. Mc-
Donald was concerned about wit-
ness’s ability to know the exact
time, and had a look at the driver’s
watch. He suggested that wit-
ness’s memory might be faulty as
to the time of day—or night.

“I put it to you,” Mr. McDonald
said, “that you remember things
you like to remember. . . . Do you
only remember things that please
your superiors?”

Witness was later asked what
his religion was, and as he failed
to understand the question, he was
asked if he believed in a God. He
appeared puzzled and gave no
reply.

Testifying as to his own part in
the alleged tossing of the beggar
into the creek, the chauffeur said
that he saw the foreigners carry-
ing the body to the rail, but he had
his face in his arms over the steer-
ing wheel and did not actually see
the body hit the water, though he
heard the splash. The dog, he said,
remained in the car and was jump-
ing about. It was raining quite
hard at the time, and was cold.

A Comfortable Place

“How long were the foreigners
away from the car to toss the
beggar in?” he was asked by Mr.
McDonald. He said he thought it
was about three or four minutes.
When they returned, he was or-
dered to drive back to the station.

“Don’t you think the running
board of a car is a comfortable
and sensible place to carry any-
body?” Mr. McDonald asked. “I’ve
tried it myself and found it so.”

Later the driver denied that
Sergeant Peters had told him to
drive to St. Luke’s Hospital.

Witness was unable to indentify
a beggar-boat such as are said to
ply up and down Hongkew Creek.
He saw no such boats in the creek
at the time, anyway, he said as
he remained in the car.

“I put it to you,” Mr. McDonald
said, “that Sergeant Peters and

《字林西报》，1936年2月6日，星期四

警察司机在两名外籍巡长审判案中
整日出庭作证

证人就斐伦路乞丐被控谋杀案接受严酷盘问；
司机坚持初级法庭时的供词

案件将于今晨继续审理；三名证人出庭作证

“今天这么多人问我这么多问题，我都不知道该说什么了！”

昨天下午，在英国驻华最高法院的证人席上，中国巡捕第3067号杜松福（Doo Sung-foo，音译）对莫索普（A. G. Mossop）法官说出这番话时，已是摇摇欲坠，由翻译转述。经过上午和下午庭审时段在证人席上长达数小时的严酷盘问后，这名警察司机突发重病，不得不在下午6点左右离开法庭几分钟，随后审讯才得以继续。翻译本人也疲惫不堪，不得不换人接替。

在针对工部局警务处（S.M.P.）巡长E. W. 彼得斯（E. W. Peters）和见习巡长W. A. 贾德（W. A. Judd）被控于12月1日上午谋杀中国乞丐毛德标（Mau Teh-piau，音译）一案的审判中，这名司机昨天大部分时间都在证人席上。作为一名不懂英语的山东人，他静静地站立数小时，回答控方和辩方律师以及法官通过翻译提出的问题，就那个命运攸关的夜晚发生的事件提供证词。据称，被告在那晚将一名生病的中国乞丐抱起，故意将其扔过外滩栏杆，抛入虹口港。司机并非当天唯一作证的证人，但他占据了大部分时间。

法庭座无虚席

尽管天气恶劣潮湿，但在诉讼的第二天，法庭内依然像第一天一样座无虚席。由12名英国居民组成的陪审团在阿斯特豪斯酒店（Astor House Hotel，即浦江饭店）过夜后，尽管时间流逝，仍非常专注，仔细跟随皇家检察官维克多·普里斯特伍德先生（Mr. Victor Priestwood，由约翰·麦克尼尔先生协助）以及辩方罗纳德·麦克唐纳先生（Mr. Ronald McDonald）和H. A. 雷克先生（Mr. H. A. Reck）所提出的证词中的细微细节。

法庭于上午9点45分开庭，中午12点30分休庭，下午2点15分复庭，并于下午6点45分结束当天的审理。案件将于今天上午9点45分继续审理，届时司机将再次出庭作证。

昨天的第一位证人是嘉兴路警署的中国电话接线员阮旺生（Yuen Wang-sheng，音译）。他作证说，12月1日凌晨2点45分，他接到来自中国巡捕第1728号的电话消息，称“一名乞丐躺在新记浜路（Sinkeipang Road，音译），情况非常危急”。中国巡捕第1728号前一天已就此作证，当晚他与第1193号巡捕一同巡逻。

证人宣称，该报告被转达给当时在警署值班室负责的彼得斯巡长。他告诉在场的马科维茨基（Makovetsky，音译）巡长去调查此案，但改变了主意，因为刚从巡逻回来的贾德巡长说了一句话，据证词称是：马科维茨基巡长，彼得斯“已经见过这个中国乞丐了”。证人称，随后彼得斯和贾德离开了值班室，后者带着一只狗，登上了由中国巡捕第3067号驾驶的警署汽车。

驾驶警署汽车

随后，这名司机登上证人席，并在那里度过了当天剩余的时间，他被普遍视为控方的关键证人。杜某陈述，他在上海当警察已超过五年，大部分时间在嘉兴路警署，现年33岁。此前他曾是一名铜匠。他身着制服出庭。

他驾驶的汽车是一辆福特旅行款车型，挂有发光的工部局（S.M.C.）牌照，号码为8502，装有两个前大灯。在事发当天早晨，两名外籍警官上了他的车，从警署出发，转入乌拉尔路（Urga Road，即今海拉尔路附近区域，注：此处Urga Road通常指海拉尔路或与其平行路段，结合下文passing Hailar Road，可能指特定路段或旧称，依原文保留或按当时习惯，此处Urga常译为乌兰巴托路或沿用旧称，但结合上下文经过海拉尔路到达Point Road，暂按音译或当时路名处理，上海地图中Urga Rd即今海拉尔路一段，但原文写passing Hailar Road，故保留原文路名逻辑），经过海拉尔路（Hailar Road），来到波因特路（Point Road，音译，即今通州路一带或特定路段），沿该路行驶至新记浜路（Sinkeipang Road）。

“当我在那里停车时，两个外国人都下了车。他们走到车后。我看见他们抬着一个乞丐朝车子走来。他们在一条弄堂的入口处把他抬起来。一个人扶着乞丐的一只胳膊，另一个人扶着乞丐的另一只胳膊。狗跟在后面。当他们来到车旁时，乞丐从鼻子里发出声音，像‘呼，呼！’”

检察官和法官都试图模仿这种声音，但效果不佳。

放在挡泥板上

“我看不清乞丐是否能走路，”证人继续说道，“两个外国人把他放在挡泥板上，头在前，脚在后。”上半身放在前挡泥板上，下半身放在踏板上。

彼得斯站在踏板上，贾德坐在车后部牵着狗。车子开到汉伯里路（Hanbury Road，即今安庆路），右转进入南京路（Nanzing Road，即今南京东路）。当皇家检察官询问司机为何朝这个方向行驶时，他回答说，他朝虹口方向开是因为“那是他们通常送乞丐去的地方”。

彼得斯告诉司机在南京路的拐角处停车，并“改变”车的“方向”，他的意思是“掉头”。“他想让我朝斐伦路（Fearon Road，即今溧阳路）开。然后他们开车到了斐伦路上余杭路桥和海宁路桥之间的一个地点，司机再次被告知在‘距离栏杆大约三四步’的地方停车。”

证人说，外国人下了车，“把乞丐抬下来”，抓住他的胳膊和腿。“抓住他之后，他们朝着车子刚才行驶的方向走了几步。他们把他头朝下扔进了河里！”

法庭要求对此进行演示。

下午庭审

下午的庭审致力于对所有这些证据进行仔细审查，并进行了大量的交叉质询。普里斯特伍德先生就细节问题盘问了司机一段时间。麦克唐纳先生关心证人知晓确切时间的能力，并查看了司机的手表。他指出，证人对白天或夜晚的时间记忆可能有误。

“我想问你，”麦克唐纳先生说，“你只记得你喜欢记得的事情……你只记得让你的上级高兴的事情吗？”

证人后来被问及他的宗教信仰是什么，由于他不理解这个问题，又被问他是否相信上帝。他显得很困惑，没有回答。

在就自己在所谓将乞丐扔进河里的行为中所扮演的角色作证时，司机说，他看见外国人将尸体抬到栏杆处，但他把脸埋在手臂里趴在方向盘上，并没有亲眼看到尸体击中水面，尽管他听到了落水声。他说，狗留在车里，跳来跳去。当时雨下得很大，天气很冷。

一个舒适的地方

“外国人离开车子把乞丐扔下去花了多长时间？”麦克唐纳先生问道。他说他认为大约是三到四分钟。当他们回来时，他受命开车返回警署。

“你不认为汽车的踏板是运送任何人的舒适且合理的地方吗？”麦克唐纳先生问。“我自己试过，发现确实如此。”

后来，司机否认彼得斯巡长曾命令他开车去圣卢克医院（St. Luke’s Hospital，即今同仁医院旧址）。

证人无法辨认出据称在虹口港上下往来的乞丐船。他说，反正当时他待在车里，没有看到河里有这样的船。

“我想问你，”麦克唐纳先生说，“彼得斯巡长和贾德巡长带着乞丐走到外滩栏杆处，将他从下栏杆下方放入下面的一艘乞丐船中。”

“我没看到那样做，”司机宣称。

后来，证人被问到：“当那个人被扔过栏杆时，你认为他会淹死吗？”

“我不知道，”他说。“我认为没有人会把另一个人扔进河里！”

司机大约在此时感到不适，不得不休息片刻。他刚刚结束了关于车辆行驶路线的仔细盘问。

证人再次回到证人席，神情紧张、脸色苍白，他说，第二天，即12月2日，他曾向嘉兴路警署的贝内特（Bennett，音译）巡官报告了此事。

THE SHANGHAI TIMES, WEDNESDAY, FEBRUARY 5, 1936

Trial Of Policemen For
Murder Of Beggar Opens
Before H.M. Court Jury

Malice Aforethought May Be Implied From Cruel
Deliberate Act, Crown Advocate Declares;
First Prosecution Witnesses Called

STORY OF HOW MAN WAS TOSSED IN
HONGKEW CREEK IS REITERATED

"Murder occurs when a person of sound memory and discretion . . . unlawfully kills any reasonable creature . . . under the King's peace, with malice aforethought either express or implied."

This was the definition of the term "murder" given by Mr. Victor Priestwood, Crown Advocate, in H. B. M. Supreme Court yesterday morning at the opening of the trial of Sergeant Ernest William Peters and Probationary Sergeant William Alfred Judd, of the Shanghai Municipal Police, on the indictment of the murder of Mau Teh-piao, a Chinese beggar.

The murder is alleged to have been committed on December 1, and the prisoners are charged with having thrown the beggar into Hongkew Creek, thereby causing his death from pneumonia.

"Malice aforethought" does not mean malice in the everyday sense of the word, Mr. Priestwood told the 12 jurors yesterday. It means an intention to commit the act, a voluntary act, intentional and unprovoked. The law may imply it by a deliberate, cruel act committed by one person against another. It may be murder, Mr. Priestwood added, when those in charge of ill persons or imbeciles, fail to supply them with proper care, causing their death.

"If a man is suffering from a disease and another accelerate his death, such an act constitutes murder."

The opening of the trial yesterday was marked by the selection of a jury panel, the presentation in summary of the case for the prosecution, and the testimony of several witnesses. The case is being tried before Judge A. G. Mossop. The Crown Advocate is being assisted by Mr. John McNeill of Hanson's, while Mr. H. A. Reeks is appearing on behalf of Judd and Mr. Ranald McDonald is representing Peters.

Jury Selected

Twelve jurymen were selected yesterday morning from a crowded courtroom of British residents, with Registrar C. H. Haines drawing the slips from a box shaken by the clerk. Twenty names were drawn, and eight were barred by objections, mostly by Messrs. Reeks and McDonald.

The jury panel finally drawn is composed of Messrs. H. Standring, H. K. Strachan, E. A. Dearn, E. S. Hind, H. Walton, K. McKelvie, C. Trickett, R. V. Yarrow, R. K. Flowright, C. S. Kemp, N. L. Sparke and G. D. Smart.

The two prisoners stood in the dock while Mr. Priestwood began by defining murder. He followed this with an outline of the case. The following are the highlights of the allegations:

At about 3 a.m. on December 1, two Chinese police constables, attached to Kashing Road Station of the S.M.P. in the northern district, discovered a male Chinese beggar lying at the side of Point Road near Sinkinang Road. Failing to arouse the man, they phoned to their headquarters from Hailar Road, reporting the case to the clerk on duty, who passed the information on to Sergeant Peters in the charge room. Peters being relieved by another sergeant, he conferred with Judd, who had returned from patrol. Judd had previously seen the man lying in the street. Peters and Judd then called the station car, and the chauffeur, a Chinese, drove the pair to Point Road, where they got out and returned with the beggar, placing him on the running board of the car. Judd rode inside, with Peters standing on the running board, and the chauffeur drove slowly up Sinkipang Road and right into Hanbury Road and over the bridge into Nanziang Road, where he was asked where he thought he was going and told to turn round and drive to Fearon Road and along the south side of Hongkew Creek. This being done, he was stopped on Peters' orders, and there the officers got out and went a couple of paces in front of the car, each holding an arm and leg of the beggar. They leaned over the railing and threw the man into the creek. The driver saw this act and heard a splash, but did not see the man hit the water. The officers then were driven back to the station.

Hawker Saw Policemen

Continuing, Mr. Priestwood declared that a hawker living on Fearon Road rose early that day for business and saw two foreigners leaning over the creek railing with an electric torch. They then drove off in a car, but the hawker made a mental note of the car number and then looked over and saw the head of a man bobbing in the water. The hawker cried for help, ran to a boat near by, got a bamboo boat-hook and hauled the man in the water to the bunding with the aid of two other Chinese passers-by. A Chinese police constable was attracted by the scene, went to Haining Road bridge and phoned the Hongkew Police Station. An ambulance was sent and the beggar was picked up, wet, cold and groaning. He was undressed, wrapped in a blanket, and taken to the Lahk Hospital and put to bed, being in a miserable condition.

The next morning, Mr. Priestwood asserted, a nurse washed and shaved the man and put him in a small room. The man in the room was seen there that day by a Chinese detective from Hongkew Station. For a day or two, Mr. Priestwood said, there was a lack of liaison between Hongkew and Kashing Roads Stations. At the hospital, a man was suffering from pneumonia; on December 3 his condition was grave, and he died on December 6. A death certificate was issued. An autopsy was performed at the Fearon Road Mortuary by three physicians, the body was identified, and the results showed that the man died of pneumonia, possibly complicated by tuberculosis. It was a new case of pneumonia contracted not more than five days before.

Police Record Entry

A telephone record book in the Kashing Road Station charge room, Mr. Priestwood declared, was found to contain the entry, "On return the beggar had left." After considerable investigation by police, the two accused were arrested on December 3, charged with assault to commit bodily harm, and taken before Magistrate C. H. Haines in H. B. M. Police Court. After the beggar died, the charges were changed to unlawful killing. At the conclusion of the case in the lower court a month ago, the defendants were formally charged with murder and bail was withdrawn.

Evidence during yesterday afternoon's session was given first by Mr. T. W. R. Wilson, assistant land surveyor of the Fearon Road district showing the creek. He was followed by Mr. J. C. Dickson, sub-inspector of the S.M.P. and Police photographer, who had made a number of photographs of the district around Fearon Road. He was examined and cross-examined regarding the boats in the creek, the lights and the houses near by. The third witness was Mr. Chang Zung-wei, hydrographer of the Whangpoo Conservancy Board, who supervised a survey party that sounded Hongkew Creek a few days ago. He had plans to show the contour of the bottom and that the probable depth of the creek at the point in question was about five or six feet at 3 a.m. on December 1, perhaps nine feet, with a soft mud bottom.

The other witnesses during the afternoon were C. P. C. 1723 of Kashing Road Station, who said he had first discovered the sick beggar in Point Road and had reported to his station; C. P. C. 1993, who gave similar testimony, and the Chinese clerk of the charge room at the Kashing Road Station, who had received the report and passed on the information.

The case will be resumed this morning. The jury meanwhile is living in the Astor House Hotel.

（批：Jules）
（印：8 FEB. 1936）
（印：DEPUTY COMMISSIONER / CRIME BRANCH / 5 FEB. 1936）
（批：Passed on please / 5 FEB 1936）

《字林西报》，1936年2月5日，星期三

巡警因谋杀乞丐受审案
在英国法院陪审团前开庭

王室律师宣称：残酷的蓄意行为可推定存在“预谋恶意”；首批控方证人出庭作证

关于男子被抛入虹口浜的经过再次被复述

“当一名神志清醒且具备判断力的人……在国王治下，以明示或暗示的预谋恶意，非法杀害任何有理性之生物……即构成谋杀。”

昨日早晨，在上海公共租界工部局警务处警长欧内斯特·威廉·彼得斯（Ernest William Peters）和见习警长威廉·阿尔弗雷德·贾德（William Alfred Judd）因涉嫌谋杀中国乞丐茅德标（Mau Teh-piao）一案的庭审开幕时，王室律师维克多·普里斯特伍德（Victor Priestwood）先生在英国驻华最高法院给出了上述关于“谋杀”一词的定义。

据称谋杀发生于12月1日，被告被指控将这名乞丐抛入虹口浜，导致其因肺炎死亡。

普里斯特伍德先生昨日告诉12名陪审员，“预谋恶意”（malice aforethought）并非日常用语中的恶意之意。它是指实施该行为的意图，是一种自愿的、故意的且无挑衅的行为。法律可以通过一人对另一人实施的 deliberate（蓄意）、残酷的行为来推定这种恶意。普里斯特伍德先生补充说，当负责照顾病人或低能者的人未能提供适当的照料从而导致其死亡时，这也可能构成谋杀。

“如果一个人患有疾病，而另一个人加速了他的死亡，这种行为即构成谋杀。”

昨日的庭审开幕包括选定陪审团名单、控方简要陈述案情以及几名证人的作证。本案由莫索普（A. G. Mossop）法官审理。王室律师由汉森律师事务所（Hanson's）的约翰·麦克尼尔（John McNeill）先生协助，而H. A. 里克斯（H. A. Reeks）先生代表贾德出庭，拉纳德·麦克唐纳（Ranald McDonald）先生代表彼得斯出庭。

选定陪审团

昨日上午，从挤满英国居民的法庭中选出了12名陪审员，书记官C. H. 海恩斯（C. H. Haines）从书记员摇动的箱子中抽取签条。共抽取了20个名字，其中8个因异议而被排除，异议主要来自里克斯先生和麦克唐纳先生。

最终选定的陪审团名单由以下人士组成：H. Standring先生、H. K. Strachan先生、E. A. Dearn先生、E. S. Hind先生、H. Walton先生、K. McKelvie先生、C. Trickett先生、R. V. Yarrow先生、R. K. Flowright先生、C. S. Kemp先生、N. L. Sparke先生和G. D. Smart先生。

两名被告站在被告席上，此时普里斯特伍德先生开始定义谋杀罪。随后他概述了案情。以下是指控要点：

12月1日凌晨3点左右，隶属于北区嘉兴路捕房的两名华籍巡警发现一名中国男乞丐躺在新金刚路（Sinkinang Road）附近的百老汇路（Point Road）路边。由于无法唤醒该男子，他们从海拉尔路（Hailar Road）打电话向总部报告，向值班书记员汇报了情况，后者将信息转达给拘留室的彼得斯警长。彼得斯由另一名警长接替后，与刚巡逻回来的贾德商议。贾德此前曾见过该男子躺在街上。随后彼得斯和贾德叫了警局的汽车，一名华籍司机驾车将两人送到百老汇路，他们下车后将乞丐带回，将其放在汽车的踏脚板上。贾德坐在车内，彼得斯站在踏脚板上，司机沿新金刚路缓慢行驶，转入汉伯里路（Hanbury Road），过桥进入南江路（Nanziang Road）。此时有人问司机打算去哪里，并命令他掉头开往斐伦路（Fearon Road），沿着虹口浜南侧行驶。照做之后，司机按彼得斯的命令停车，两名警官下车，走到车前几步远的地方，每人抓着乞丐的一条手臂和一条腿。他们探身越过栏杆，将该男子抛入浜中。司机看到了这一行为并听到了落水声，但没有看到该男子击中水面。随后警官们被驾车送回捕房。

小贩目睹巡警

普里斯特伍德先生继续说道，当天清晨，一名住在斐伦路的小贩早起做生意，看到两名外国人打着手电筒俯身在浜边的栏杆上。随后他们驾车离开，但小贩记下了车牌号，然后回头查看，看到一个男人的头在水中起伏。小贩呼救，跑到附近的一艘船边，拿来一根竹制撑篙，并在另外两名中国路人的帮助下，将水中的男子拖到岸堤上。一名华籍巡警被现场吸引，前往海宁路桥并打电话给虹口捕房。救护车随即派出，乞丐被救起时浑身湿透、寒冷且呻吟不止。他被脱去衣物，裹在毯子里，送往乐克医院（Lahk Hospital）并安置在床上，状况极其糟糕。

普里斯特伍德先生断言，第二天早上，一名护士为该男子清洗、剃须，并将他安置在一间小房间里。当天，一名来自虹口捕房的华籍侦探在那间房间里见到了该男子。普里斯特伍德先生说，有一两天时间，虹口捕房和嘉兴路捕房之间缺乏联络。在医院里，该男子患有肺炎；12月3日他的病情危重，并于12月6日死亡。随后出具了死亡证明。三名医生在斐伦路验尸所进行了尸检，确认了尸体身份，结果显示该男子死于肺炎，可能并发肺结核。这是一例新的肺炎病例，感染时间不超过五天。

警局记录条目

普里斯特伍德先生宣称，在嘉兴路捕房拘留室的一本电话记录簿中，发现有一条记录写着：“返回时乞丐已离开。”经过警方大量调查，两名被告于12月3日被捕，被控袭击致身体伤害，并被带到英国警察法庭的海恩斯治安官面前。在乞丐死后，指控改为非法杀人。一个月前在下级法院结案时，被告被正式指控犯有谋杀罪，保释被撤销。

昨日下午庭审期间首先由斐伦路地区的助理土地测量员T. W. R. 威尔逊（T. W. R. Wilson）先生作证，展示该浜的情况。随后是上海公共租界工部局警务处副督察兼警务摄影师J. C. 迪克森（J. C. Dickson）先生，他拍摄了斐伦路周边地区的多张照片。他就浜中的船只、灯光和附近房屋接受了讯问和交叉讯问。第三位证人是黄浦浚浦局的水道测量员张宗伟（Chang Zung-wei，音译）先生，他几天前监督了一个测量队对虹口浜进行了测深。他出示了图纸以显示底部轮廓，并指出12月1日凌晨3点，争议地点的浜深约为五至六英尺，可能达到九英尺，底部为软泥。

下午的其他证人包括嘉兴路捕房的华籍巡警1723号，他说他首先在百老汇路发现了生病的乞丐并向捕房报告；华籍巡警1993号，提供了类似的证词；以及嘉兴路捕房拘留室的华籍书记员，他接收了报告并传递了信息。

案件将于今天上午继续审理。与此同时，陪审团成员住在礼查饭店（Astor House Hotel）。

（批注：Jules）

THE CHINA PRESS, MONDAY, FEBRUARY 3, 1936

Trial Of Two
S. M. Police
Opens Tuesday

Peters And Judd Charged
With Unlawful Killing
Of Chinese Beggar

The trial of Sergeant E. W. Peters
and Probationary Sergeant W. A.
Judd, of the Shanghai Municipal
Police Force, on charges of unlaw-
ful killing, will commence before the
H.M. Supreme Court tomorrow
morning. The pair are alleged to
have thrown a Chinese beggar, Pau
Teh-plau, into Hongkew Creek on
the morning of December 1, there-
by contributing to his death.
Sergeants Peters and Judd were
arrested on December 3, 1935, after
private investigation into the affair
conducted by the Shanghai Munici-
pal Police and were subsequently
brought before Magistrate C. H.
Haines in H.M. Police Court for
preliminary investigation. Mr. John
McNeill handled the case for the
prosecution while Mr. H. A. Reeks
appeared for the defendants. It is
understood that Mr. Reeks will ap-
pear for at least one of the defend-
ants during the trial.
The preliminary investigation was
a long, drawn out affair, lasting
most of the month of December.
The principal witness for the pro-
secution was a police constable who
had driven the two sergeants from
the Kashing Road Police Station to
the corner of Point and Sinkeipang
Roads where the beggar was picked
up from an alleyway and placed on
the running board of the car.
According to the chauffeur, the
two sergeants took the man from
the running board of the car on
Pearon Road and tossed him into
Hongkew Creek. He declared that
he saw the act, but did not see
the body of the beggar strike the
water. He did hear the splash,
however, he stated.
The beggar was taken from the
water, according to testimony given
down during the trial, by a Chinese
hawker, assisted by one or two com-
panions. The man was then trans-
ported to St. Luke's Hospital where
he died a few days later.
According to medical testimony
submitted, the beggar was suffering
from pneumonia. Fresh pneumonia
lesions appeared, it was pointed out,
about the time the man was thrown
into the creek and it was possible
that this new attack of pneumonia
had caused his death.
Registrar Haines bound the two
over to H.M. Supreme Court for
trial on charges of murder which
was later changed to charges of un-
lawful killing.

《大美晚报》，1936年2月3日，星期一

两名
上海公共租界
巡警审判案
周二开庭

彼得斯和贾德被控
非法杀害中国乞丐

上海公共租界工部局警务处警长E. W. 彼得斯和见习警长W. A. 贾德的非法杀人罪审判案，将于明天上午在英国最高法院开庭。据称，这两人于12月1日上午将一名中国乞丐鲍德彪（Pau Teh-plau，音译）抛入虹口浜，从而促成了他的死亡。

彼得斯警长和贾德警长是在上海公共租界工部局对该事件进行私下调查后，于1935年12月3日被捕的，随后被带到英国警察法庭的海恩斯治安官面前进行初步审讯。约翰·麦克尼尔先生代表控方处理此案，而H. A. 里克斯先生代表被告出庭。据悉，里克斯先生将在审判期间至少为其中一名被告辩护。

初步审讯是一场漫长而拖延的过程，持续了整个12月的大部分时间。控方的主要证人是一名巡警，他曾驾驶汽车载着两名警长从嘉兴路捕房前往百老汇路和新金刚路的拐角处，在那里，乞丐从一条小巷中被带出并放置在汽车的踏脚板上。

据司机称，两名警长在斐伦路将那人从汽车踏脚板上带走，并将其抛入虹口浜。他声称看到了这一行为，但没有看到乞丐的身体击中水面。不过，他表示确实听到了落水声。

根据庭审期间提供的证词，这名乞丐是由一名中国小贩在一两名同伴的协助下从水中救出的。随后该男子被送往圣路加医院（St. Luke's Hospital），几天后在那里死亡。

根据提交的医学证词，这名乞丐患有肺炎。有人指出，在该男子被抛入浜中的时候出现了新的肺炎病灶，因此这次新的肺炎发作可能导致了他的死亡。

海恩斯书记官将两人移送英国最高法院，以谋杀罪受审，后来改为非法杀人罪。

THE SHANGHAI SUNDAY TIMES, JANUARY 26, 1936

McDONALD TO DEFEND
SERGEANT PETERS
Mr. Ranald G. McDonald, well-known British barrister, will appear on behalf of Sergeant E. W. Peters, of the Shanghai Municipal Police, on February 4, when Peters, together with Probationary Sergeant W. A. Judd, S.M.P., will face the British Supreme Court on a charge of murder, of having assaulted and unlawfully killed one Mau Tuh-piau, a sick beggar, on the morning of December 1. Mr. H. A. Reeks will appear on behalf of Judd.
Peters and Judd were indicted in the British Police Court several weeks ago after a prolonged preliminary trial. They were charged then with having tossed a sick beggar they had picked up in Fearon Road into Hongkew Creek, after which the beggar died from pneumonia.
page_data.zh:
《上海星期泰晤士报》，1936年1月26日

麦克唐纳将为
彼得斯警长辩护

著名的英国大律师拉纳德·G. 麦克唐纳（Ranald G. McDonald）先生将于2月4日代表上海公共租界工部局警务处的E. W. 彼得斯警长出庭。届时，彼得斯将与上海公共租界工部局警务处的见习警长W. A. 贾德一起，在英国最高法院面对谋杀罪的指控，罪名是于12月1日上午袭击并非法杀害了一名生病的乞丐茅德彪（Mau Tuh-piau，音译）。H. A. 里克斯先生将代表贾德出庭。

彼得斯和贾德在数周前经过漫长的初步审判后，在英国警察法庭被起诉。当时他们被指控将他们在斐伦路捡到的一名生病的乞丐抛入虹口浜，随后该乞丐因肺炎死亡。

THE NORTH-CHINA DAILY NEWS, THURSDAY, JANUARY 16, 1936

MURDER TRIAL WILL
OPEN NEXT MONTH

Two Policemen to Face
Judge and Jury

FIRST HEARING SET FOR
FEBRUARY 4

The trial by judge and jury of
Sergeant, F. W. Peters, and Prob.-
Serg., W. A. Judd, against each of
whom a charge of the murder of Mau
Teh-piau has been preferred, will open
in H.M. Supreme Court on Tuesday,
February 4, at 10 a.m.

The two accused were committed
for trial by the Registrar, Mr. C. H.
Haines, on January 6, when the pre-
liminary examination into the case
was concluded. Prosecuting counsel
was Mr. John McNeill and defending
counsel Mr. H. A. Reeks. Both de-
fendants, after the charge was read
out to them, pleaded not guilty.

The case against the two accused
opened on December 4 when they
were charged with causing actual
bodily harm to Mau Te-piau, a Chi-
nese beggar, by throwing him into
Hongkew Creek. On December 6
Mau died in St. Luke's Hospital and
at an inquest which was subsequently
held, it was found that death was due
to double pneumonia complicated by
water. When the accused came up
before the Registrar for the second
time on December 10, they were
charged additionally with having
thrown Mau into Hongkew Creek and
thereby unlawfully killing him.

Sergt. Peters and Prob.-Serg. Judd
are 31 and 26 years of age respective-
ly, and were suspended during the
investigation of the case. At the
conclusion of the preliminary hearing
the Registrar informed both accused
that they would be kept in custody
pending their trial. The Crown Ad-
vocate, Mr. Victor Priestwood, will
prosecute in the forthcoming trial.

《字林西报》，1936年1月16日，星期四

谋杀案审判将于下月开庭

两名警员将面对法官与陪审团

首次聆讯定于2月4日举行

警长 F. W. Peters 和试用警长 W. A. Judd 被控谋杀毛德标（Mau Teh-piau），针对二人的案件将由法官与陪审团审理，并于2月4日星期二上午10时在大英按察使司衙门（H.M. Supreme Court）开庭。

两名被告于1月6日由书记官 C. H. Haines 先生交付审判，当时对该案的初步审讯已告结束。控方律师为 John McNeill 先生，辩方律师为 H. A. Reeks 先生。在向两名被告宣读指控后，二人均表示不认罪。

针对两名被告的案件于12月4日展开，当时他们被控将一名中国乞丐毛德标（Mau Te-piau）抛入虹口港，致其遭受实际身体伤害。12月6日，毛在圣路加医院去世，随后举行的死因研讯认定，死因为并发积水的双侧肺炎。12月10日，当被告第二次出庭受审于书记官面前时，又被追加指控将毛抛入虹口港，从而非法将其杀害。

Peters 警长和 Judd 试用警长分别为31岁和26岁，在案件调查期间已被停职。在初步聆讯结束时，书记官告知两名被告，在候审期间他们将一直被羁押。皇家大律师 Victor Priestwood 先生将在即将到来的审判中担任控方。

THE SHANGHAI TIMES, TUESDAY, JANUARY 7, 1936

Policemen Will Be Tried
On Charge Of Murder

Accused Make Statements They Put Man On “Beggar
Boat” In Creek; Bail Withdrawn Pending
Application In H. M. Supreme Court

S.M.P. Sergeant E. W. Peters and Probationary Sergeant W. A. Judd will be tried before H. M. Supreme Court on a charge of murder in the case of Mau Tuh-piau, a beggar, whom they are alleged to have thrown into Hongkew Creek on the early morning of December 1, according to the decision made yesterday morning by Mr. C. H. Haines, H. M. Magistrate, before whom they were examined and the case of the prosecution presented.

In committing them for trial on a charge of murder, Mr. Haines stated that in view of his decision the matter of bail had been taken out of his hands and the men would be kept in custody pending trial. Mr. Reeks, for the defence, said he would make an application for bail in the upper court.

The identic charges against the two men read: “That you at Shanghai on December 1, 1935, murdered Mau Tuh-piau.”

“Not guilty,” the two men responded to the charge.

Mr. H. A. Reeks, counsel for the defence, said that their case would be reserved for the upper court but said they would each like to make a short statement. They were accordingly cautioned and their statements taken down. Standing in the dock they then made their first statements to the court in connection with the incident.

Put Beggar On Boat

Sergeant Peters said that shortly after 2.44 a.m. on December 1 he had accompanied Sergeant Judd to pick up a sick beggar lying at the corner of Point and Singkeipang Roads. They put him on the car and started for St. Luke’s Hospital, but on the way the beggar seemed to revive. Inasmuch as St. Luke’s Hospital did not take cases of beggars unless they were very serious ones he had the car turned back along Fearon Road so that the beggar might be put on one of the “beggar boats” lying in Hongkew Creek. They did not throw the beggar into the creek, he said, but placed him on one of the boats, and he was there when they left.

Sergeant Peters explained his decision to go with Sergeant Judd for the reason that Judd had but recently been transferred to Kashing Road district and did not know the streets.

The statement of Sergeant Judd was similar to that of Peters.

Died In Hospital

Following legal argument by Mr. Reeks on the admissibility of evidence, points which Mr. Haines said he would note in the record, the police court inquiry was adjourned.

A brief résumé of the case for the prosecution is that the sick beggar was noted at the corner of Point and Singkeipang Roads about 2.45 a.m. by a Chinese constable, who telephoned the matter to Kashing Road Station. Sergeant Peters left his duty to go with Judd by car to the place. They picked up the beggar, put him on the running board and after driving around went into Fearon Road, stopped the car and threw the man into Hongkew Creek. A hawker and several other people saved the man and a police constable from Hongkew Station got an ambulance which took the beggar to St. Luke’s Hospital, where he died several days later from double pneumonia.

File
JAS
'37 Jan
